Turn this wide table of marks into a long one with columns student, subject, mark, and then compute the mean mark per subject.

Answer

Exercise 6

Why is replacing missing ages with the mean age a questionable choice for a study of how spending varies with age?

Answer

It puts all the customers with unknown age at one value, the mean, which creates an artificial cluster there and weakens any real relationship between age and spending. It also understates the spread of ages. Dropping those customers (if few), or flagging them and checking whether they differ in spending, is more defensible; whichever is chosen should be reported.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction
docs.text:
Finding groups and structure in data without labels

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain what unsupervised learning is and what it can and cannot tell you;
  • describe the k-means algorithm, run it with scikit-learn, and explain why features must be scaled;
  • choose the number of clusters with the elbow method and the silhouette score, and know their limits;
  • describe agglomerative (hierarchical) clustering and read a dendrogram;
  • explain principal component analysis (PCA) as finding directions of greatest variance;
  • use PCA to reduce dimensions and to plot high-dimensional data, and read its explained variance and loadings;
  • carry out and interpret a customer segmentation.

Chapters 8 to 10 were about supervised learning: every training example came with the right answer. Often there is no answer to learn from. A shop has data on its customers but no label saying which "type" each is; a scientist has hundreds of measurements per sample and wants to see the main patterns. Unsupervised learning looks for structure in the features alone. This chapter covers its two main tasks: clustering, which groups similar examples, and dimensionality reduction, which summarises many features by a few.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

docs.title: 11.1 What clustering is for
docs.text:
A cluster is a group of examples that are more similar to each other than to examples in other groups. Clustering is used to find customer segments for marketing, to group documents by topic, to spot unusual cases (those that fit no cluster well), and to compress data by replacing each example with its cluster's representative.

There is a fundamental difference from classification: there is no right answer to check against. Different algorithms, different features or different scalings give different clusterings, and none is "correct". A clustering is judged by whether its groups are compact and well separated, which can be measured, and by whether they are useful and interpretable for the purpose at hand, which only a person who knows the domain can judge.

Caution: clustering always finds clusters

Ask k-means for four clusters and it returns four clusters, even for data with no group structure at all. The existence of an output is no evidence that the groups are real. Check with plots, with the measures of Section 11.3, and by seeing whether the groups are stable when the data or the settings change slightly.

docs.title: 11.2 k-means
docs.text:
k-means is the most widely used clustering algorithm. You choose the number of clusters \(k\). Each cluster is represented by its centroid, the mean of its members, and k-means seeks the centroids that minimise the total squared distance from each point to its nearest centroid, called the inertia (or within-cluster sum of squares):

\[ \text{inertia} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert x_i - \mu_{c(i)} \rVert^2 , \]

where \(\mu_{c(i)}\) is the centroid of the cluster to which example \(i\) is assigned. The standard algorithm alternates two steps:

  1. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
  2. Update each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it.

It starts from initial centroids (scikit-learn uses a careful random choice called k-means++) and repeats the two steps until the assignments stop changing. Each step can only lower the inertia, so the algorithm always stops, but possibly at a local minimum that depends on the starting centroids. scikit-learn therefore runs it several times from different starts (n_init) and keeps the best result.

Example 11.1: One round of k-means by hand

Six points on a line: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 14, with \(k = 2\) and starting centroids 1 and 2.

  • Assign: 1 is nearest to centroid 1; 2, 3, 10, 11, 14 are nearest to centroid 2 (or tied, for 2 itself, which goes to centroid 2).
  • Update: centroid 1 becomes the mean of {1}, which is 1; centroid 2 becomes the mean of {2, 3, 10, 11, 14}, which is 8.
  • Assign: 1 and 2 are nearer to 1 than to 8; 3 is at distance 2 from 1 and 5 from 8, so it joins the first cluster; 10, 11, 14 go to 8.
  • Update: centroids become \((1 + 2 + 3)/3 = 2\) and \((10 + 11 + 14)/3 = 11.67\).
  • Assign: nothing changes, so the algorithm stops with clusters {1, 2, 3} and {10, 11, 14}.
pts = np.array([1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 14]).reshape(-1, 1)
km = KMeans(n_clusters=2, init=np.array([[1.0], [2.0]]), n_init=1).fit(pts)
print(km.labels_, km.cluster_centers_.ravel().round(2), round(km.inertia_, 2))

[0 0 0 1 1 1] [ 2.   11.67] 10.67

The inertia is \((1-2)^2 + 0 + (3-2)^2 + (10-11.67)^2 + (11-11.67)^2 + (14-11.67)^2 = 2 + 8.67 = 10.67\).

docs.title: k-means on two-dimensional data
docs.text:
We generate 300 points in three groups of different sizes, so that we can see whether k-means recovers them.

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
centres = np.array([[2, 2], [7, 3], [4, 8]])
sizes = [120, 100, 80]
pts2 = np.vstack([rng.normal(c, 1.0, size=(s, 2)) for c, s in zip(centres, sizes)])
true_group = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], sizes)

km3 = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(pts2)
print(km3.cluster_centers_.round(2))
print(pd.crosstab(true_group, km3.labels_, rownames=["true"], colnames=["cluster"]))

[[7.11 3.16]
 [1.98 2.06]
 [3.99 8.28]]
cluster   0    1   2
true                
0         0  120   0
1        99    1   0
2         0    1  79

The crosstab compares the found clusters with the true groups. The cluster numbers are arbitrary (cluster 0 need not be group 0), but each true group falls almost entirely into one cluster, with a few points near the borders assigned to a neighbour.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
axes[0].scatter(pts2[:, 0], pts2[:, 1], s=12, color="gray")
axes[0].set_title("The data, without labels")
axes[1].scatter(pts2[:, 0], pts2[:, 1], c=km3.labels_, s=12, cmap="viridis")
axes[1].scatter(km3.cluster_centers_[:, 0], km3.cluster_centers_[:, 1], marker="X", s=200,
                color="red", edgecolor="white", label="centroids")
axes[1].set_title("k-means with k = 3")
axes[1].legend()
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("feature 1")
axes[0].set_ylabel("feature 2")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("kmeans.svg")
Figure 11.1 k-means finds three clusters. Left: 300 points in gray forming three visible clouds. Right: the same points coloured by the k-means cluster they were assigned to, with the three centroids marked by large red crosses at the centres of the clouds.

docs.title: Scale matters
docs.text:
k-means uses Euclidean distances, so, as with k-NN, a feature with a large range dominates. If one feature is income in rupees (tens of thousands) and another is age in years (tens), the clustering is essentially a clustering by income alone. Standardise the features first unless they are already on comparable scales and those scales are meaningful.

k-means also assumes, in effect, that clusters are roughly round and of similar spread, because it assigns each point to the nearest centroid. It handles elongated, curved or very unequal clusters poorly; other algorithms (Section 11.4) do better there.

docs.title: 11.3 Choosing the number of clusters
docs.text:
k-means needs \(k\), but the data does not come labelled with it. Two common aids:

The elbow method plots the inertia against \(k\). Inertia always falls as \(k\) grows (with \(k = n\) it is zero), so the minimum is useless; instead look for an "elbow" where adding another cluster stops helping much.

The silhouette score measures how well each point fits its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster. For a point \(i\), let \(a(i)\) be its average distance to the other points of its cluster and \(b(i)\) its average distance to the points of the nearest other cluster. Its silhouette is

\[ s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max(a(i),\, b(i))}, \]

which lies between \(-1\) and \(1\): near 1 means well inside its cluster, near 0 means on a border, negative means probably in the wrong cluster. The silhouette score is the average over all points; higher is better.

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

ks = range(2, 9)
inertias, silhouettes = [], []
for k in ks:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(pts2)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(pts2, km.labels_))
    print(f"k={k}: inertia {km.inertia_:8.1f}, silhouette {silhouettes[-1]:.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
axes[0].plot(list(ks), inertias, marker="o")
axes[0].set_xlabel("number of clusters k")
axes[0].set_ylabel("inertia")
axes[0].set_title("Elbow method")
axes[1].plot(list(ks), silhouettes, marker="o", color="tab:green")
axes[1].set_xlabel("number of clusters k")
axes[1].set_ylabel("mean silhouette")
axes[1].set_title("Silhouette score")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("choosing-k.svg")

k=2: inertia   2071.9, silhouette 0.511
k=3: inertia    573.9, silhouette 0.669
k=4: inertia    486.3, silhouette 0.516
k=5: inertia    419.8, silhouette 0.420
k=6: inertia    365.0, silhouette 0.426
k=7: inertia    318.7, silhouette 0.432
k=8: inertia    282.8, silhouette 0.328
Figure 11.2 The elbow method and the silhouette score. Left: inertia falls steeply from k = 2 to k = 3 and then much more slowly, giving an elbow at k = 3. Right: the mean silhouette score is highest at k = 3 and lower for every other k.

Both point to \(k = 3\), the true number. With real data the signals are rarely so clear; then the choice of \(k\) is made by combining these measures with the purpose of the analysis (how many segments can the marketing team actually use?).

docs.title: 11.4 Hierarchical clustering
docs.text:
Agglomerative clustering builds a hierarchy of clusters from the bottom up. It starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until only one remains. "Closest" between clusters is defined by a linkage rule: single linkage uses the closest pair of points, complete linkage the farthest pair, average linkage the average distance, and Ward's method merges the pair whose merger increases the within-cluster sum of squares least (the same criterion as k-means).

The whole merging history is drawn as a dendrogram, a tree in which the height of each join shows the distance at which the two clusters merged. Cutting the tree at a chosen height gives a clustering; long vertical stretches with no merges suggest natural places to cut. SciPy draws dendrograms; here are 30 of the points:

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

sub_idx = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(pts2), 30, replace=False)
sub = pts2[sub_idx]
Z = linkage(sub, method="ward")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.5))
dendrogram(Z, ax=ax, labels=true_group[sub_idx], color_threshold=8)
ax.set_xlabel("points (labelled by their true group)")
ax.set_ylabel("merge distance")
ax.set_title("Dendrogram (Ward linkage), 30 points")
fig.savefig("dendrogram.svg")

agg = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage="ward").fit(pts2)
print(pd.crosstab(true_group, agg.labels_, rownames=["true"], colnames=["cluster"]))

cluster    0   1   2
true                
0        120   0   0
1          2   0  98
2          1  79   0
Figure 11.3 A dendrogram. A dendrogram of 30 points. Leaves at the bottom are labelled 0, 1 or 2 by true group. Small merges near the bottom join points of the same group; three main branches, each containing mostly one label, join only at large heights near the top, so cutting the tree below those last merges gives three clusters.

Agglomerative clustering does not need \(k\) in advance (the dendrogram shows all choices), and with single linkage it can find long, curved clusters that k-means cannot. It is slower on large datasets, because it compares all pairs of clusters. DBSCAN, also in scikit-learn, is another alternative: it defines clusters as dense regions separated by sparse ones, finds clusters of any shape, and labels isolated points as noise instead of forcing them into a cluster.

docs.title: 11.5 Principal component analysis
docs.text:
Datasets often have many features, some of them strongly related. Ten measurements of a person's body are largely driven by overall size; dozens of survey answers may reflect a few underlying attitudes. Dimensionality reduction replaces many features with a few new ones that keep most of the information. It helps with plotting (we can only see two or three dimensions), with speed, and sometimes with model performance.

Principal component analysis (PCA) finds new axes, the principal components, that are combinations of the original features:

  • the first component is the direction along which the data varies most;
  • the second is the direction of greatest remaining variance at right angles to the first;
  • and so on, each at right angles to all the earlier ones.

Projecting the data onto the first few components gives a lower-dimensional version that keeps as much of the variance as possible. Each component has an explained variance ratio, the share of the total variance it captures, and loadings, the weights of the original features in it.

A small example shows the idea in two dimensions. Height and arm span are strongly correlated, so most of the variation lies along one diagonal direction, "overall size":

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
size = rng.normal(0, 1, 200)
body = pd.DataFrame({"height": 170 + 8 * size + rng.normal(0, 2, 200),
                     "arm_span": 171 + 8.5 * size + rng.normal(0, 2, 200)})
body_std = StandardScaler().fit_transform(body)
pca2 = PCA().fit(body_std)
print("explained variance ratio:", pca2.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))
print("loadings (rows = components):")
print(pd.DataFrame(pca2.components_, columns=body.columns, index=["PC1", "PC2"]).round(3))

explained variance ratio: [0.966 0.034]
loadings (rows = components):
     height  arm_span
PC1   0.707     0.707
PC2  -0.707     0.707

The first component captures nearly all the variance, and its loadings weight height and arm span equally (the overall sign of a component is arbitrary): it is "size". The second, a contrast between the two (long arms for one's height, or short), carries little. One number per person, the PC1 score, keeps almost everything the two measurements say.

Key idea

PCA rotates the data to new axes ordered by how much the data varies along them, so that the first few axes carry most of the information. It is unsupervised: it looks only at the features, not at any target, so the directions of greatest variance are not necessarily the most useful for prediction.

As with k-means, standardise first: PCA chases variance, and a feature measured in large units has a large variance purely because of its units.

docs.title: 11.6 Worked example: customer segments
docs.text:
A shop has six measurements for each of 400 customers over a year: total spend, number of visits, average basket value, days since the last visit (recency), share of purchases made online, and number of distinct product categories bought. It wants a handful of segments to plan its marketing. We simulate customers from four underlying types (which, in reality, nobody would know).

rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
types = {   # visits, basket, recency, online share, categories
    "frequent small": (60, 300, 5, 0.1, 6),
    "occasional big": (8, 2500, 40, 0.3, 4),
    "online regular": (30, 700, 10, 0.9, 8),
    "lapsed": (3, 500, 200, 0.2, 2),
}
rows = []
for name, (visits, basket, recency, online, cats) in types.items():
    m = 100
    v = rng.poisson(visits, m) + 1
    b = rng.normal(basket, basket * 0.25, m).clip(50)
    rows.append(pd.DataFrame({
        "visits": v, "basket": b.round(0), "spend": (v * b).round(0),
        "recency": rng.normal(recency, recency * 0.4 + 2, m).clip(0).round(0),
        "online_share": rng.beta(online * 20 + 1, (1 - online) * 20 + 1, m).round(2),
        "categories": rng.poisson(cats, m) + 1,
        "true_type": name}))
shop = pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)
features = ["spend", "visits", "basket", "recency", "online_share", "categories"]
print(shop[features].describe().round(1).loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]])

        spend  visits  basket  recency  online_share  categories
mean  16044.9    26.0   987.5     61.5           0.4         5.9
std   10476.3    22.7   910.8     90.1           0.3         3.1
min     238.0     1.0   121.0      0.0           0.0         1.0
max   46798.0    84.0  3591.0    437.0           1.0        16.0

The features are on wildly different scales (spend in tens of thousands, online share between 0 and 1), so we standardise, then look at the explained variance of PCA to see how much structure a two-dimensional picture can show:

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(shop[features])
pca = PCA().fit(Xs)
print("explained variance ratio:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))
print("cumulative:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum().round(3))

explained variance ratio: [0.441 0.259 0.177 0.064 0.05  0.008]
cumulative: [0.441 0.7   0.877 0.941 0.992 1.   ]

The first two components carry about 70% of the variance, enough for a useful picture. We choose \(k\) with the silhouette score, cluster in the full standardised space, and plot the clusters on the first two components:

for k in range(2, 8):
    lab = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xs)
    print(f"k={k}: silhouette {silhouette_score(Xs, lab):.3f}")

k=2: silhouette 0.376
k=3: silhouette 0.457
k=4: silhouette 0.557
k=5: silhouette 0.508
k=6: silhouette 0.462
k=7: silhouette 0.414

km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(Xs)
shop["segment"] = km.labels_
scores2 = pca.transform(Xs)[:, :2]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
for seg in range(4):
    m = shop["segment"] == seg
    ax.scatter(scores2[m, 0], scores2[m, 1], s=12, label=f"segment {seg}")
ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.0%} of variance)")
ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.0%} of variance)")
ax.set_title("Customer segments on the first two principal components")
ax.legend()
fig.savefig("segments-pca.svg")
print(pd.crosstab(shop["true_type"], shop["segment"]))

segment           0    1   2    3
true_type                        
frequent small    0    0   0  100
lapsed            0  100   0    0
occasional big    0    1  99    0
online regular  100    0   0    0
Figure 11.4 Four customer segments seen through PCA. A scatter plot of 400 customers on the first two principal components, coloured by k-means segment. Four distinct, compact groups of points are visible, each a single colour, with little overlap between them.

The silhouette score points to four clusters, and each found segment corresponds almost exactly to one of the hidden customer types. The last and most important step is to profile the segments, describing each in the language of the business, because the cluster numbers mean nothing by themselves:

profile = shop.groupby("segment")[features].median().round(1)
profile["customers"] = shop["segment"].value_counts().sort_index()
print(profile)

           spend  visits  basket  recency  online_share  categories  customers
segment                                                                       
0        21522.5    31.0   663.5      8.0           0.9         9.0        100
1         1814.0     4.0   512.0    192.0           0.2         3.0        101
2        20763.0     9.0  2529.0     39.0           0.3         5.0         99
3        18531.0    60.0   311.0      5.0           0.1         7.0        100

Reading the medians, the segments can be named: frequent visitors with small baskets; occasional visitors with large baskets and the highest spend per visit; online regulars buying across many categories; and lapsed customers with very long recency. Each suggests a different action: loyalty rewards, offers on large purchases, online promotions, a win-back campaign. That interpretation, not the algorithm, is the result of the analysis.

docs.title: 11.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels. A clustering has no single correct answer; judge it by compactness, separation, stability and usefulness.
  • k-means alternates assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to the mean, minimising inertia; it finds local minima, so it is run from several starts (n_init).
  • Standardise features before distance-based methods. k-means suits roughly round clusters of similar spread.
  • Choose \(k\) with the elbow of the inertia curve and the silhouette score \(s = (b - a)/\max(a, b)\), combined with the purpose of the analysis.
  • Agglomerative clustering merges the closest clusters step by step under a linkage rule; the dendrogram shows every level. DBSCAN finds dense regions of any shape and marks noise.
  • PCA finds orthogonal directions of greatest variance; the explained variance ratio says how much each keeps, and the loadings say what it is made of. Standardise first.
  • Profile clusters in domain terms; that interpretation is the real result.

docs.title: 11.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Run k-means by hand on the points 2, 4, 5, 12, 13, 20 with \(k = 2\) and starting centroids 2 and 20. Give the final clusters and centroids.

Answer

Assign: 2, 4, 5 are nearer to 2; 12 is at distance 10 from 2 and 8 from 20, so it goes to 20, as do 13 and 20. Update: centroids \((2 + 4 + 5)/3 = 3.67\) and \((12 + 13 + 20)/3 = 15\). Assign again: 12 is at distance 8.33 from 3.67 and 3 from 15, so nothing changes. Final clusters {2, 4, 5} and {12, 13, 20}.

p = np.array([2, 4, 5, 12, 13, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)
r = KMeans(n_clusters=2, init=np.array([[2.0], [20.0]]), n_init=1).fit(p)
print(r.labels_, r.cluster_centers_.ravel().round(2))

[0 0 0 1 1 1] [ 3.67 15.  ]

Exercise 2

A point has average distance 2.0 to the other members of its cluster and 5.0 to the members of the nearest other cluster. What is its silhouette? What if the distances were 4.0 and 3.0?

Answer

\(s = (5 - 2)/5 = 0.6\): it sits comfortably in its cluster. With \(a = 4\) and \(b = 3\), \(s = (3 - 4)/4 = -0.25\): it is closer on average to the other cluster and is probably misassigned.

Exercise 3

Cluster the shop data with \(k = 4\) without standardising the features first. Compare the result with the true types and explain what happens.

Answer 
raw_km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(shop[features])
print(pd.crosstab(shop["true_type"], raw_km.labels_))

col_0            0    1   2   3
true_type                      
frequent small  45    5  48   2
lapsed           0  100   0   0
occasional big  34    6  32  28
online regular  51    2  37  10

Without scaling, spend (tens of thousands) dominates every distance and the other features hardly matter, so the clusters are essentially bands of spend that cut across the true types. Standardising lets all six features contribute.

Exercise 4

In a PCA of 10 standardised features, the explained variance ratios of the first three components are 0.52, 0.21 and 0.09. How much variance do two components keep? How many components are needed to keep at least 80%?

Answer

Two components keep \(0.52 + 0.21 = 0.73\), or 73%. Three keep \(0.82\), so three components are needed for at least 80%.

Exercise 5

Why is it wrong to say that the "best" clustering of a dataset is the one with the lowest inertia?

Answer

Inertia always decreases as the number of clusters grows, reaching zero when every point is its own cluster, so minimising it simply means using as many clusters as possible. Inertia can compare clusterings only for the same \(k\); choosing \(k\) needs another criterion (an elbow, the silhouette, or the purpose of the analysis).

Exercise 6

A colleague runs PCA on customer data and finds that PC1 has large positive loadings on spend, visits and categories. How might you describe PC1 in words, and why should you be careful with its sign?

Answer

PC1 is something like "overall engagement" or "activity": customers with high scores spend more, visit more often and buy across more categories. The sign of a component is arbitrary (the same direction pointing the other way is an equally valid component), so a different program or run might give the opposite signs; the interpretation depends on the pattern of loadings, not on whether they are positive or negative.

docs.title: 11.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 11

Exercise 1

Which statement about k-means is true?

  1. it needs labelled data
  2. it needs the number of clusters in advance
  3. it always finds the global minimum of inertia
  4. it does not use distances
Answer

it needs the number of clusters in advance

Exercise 2

Why does scikit-learn run k-means several times (n_init)?

  1. to use more data
  2. because the result depends on the starting centroids
  3. to compute the silhouette
  4. to scale the features
Answer

because the result depends on the starting centroids

Exercise 3

A silhouette value close to -1 means the point is

  1. well inside its cluster
  2. on the border between clusters
  3. probably in the wrong cluster
  4. an outlier with no cluster
Answer

probably in the wrong cluster

Exercise 4

The first principal component is the direction of

  1. the target
  2. greatest variance
  3. least variance
  4. the first feature
Answer

greatest variance

Exercise 5

Before k-means or PCA on features measured in different units you should

  1. standardise them
  2. sort them
  3. one-hot encode them
  4. remove the mean only from the target
Answer

standardise them

Exercise 6

What is the name of the tree diagram that shows the merges of hierarchical clustering?

Answer

dendrogram / a dendrogram

Exercise 7

Inertia, as the number of clusters k increases,

  1. always decreases or stays the same
  2. always increases
  3. is unchanged
  4. has a minimum at the true k
Answer

always decreases or stays the same

docs.title: Chapter 13: Ethics, Privacy and Reproducibility
docs.text:
Doing data science that is fair to people and that others can check

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why ethical questions arise at every stage of the data science workflow;
  • distinguish direct identifiers from quasi-identifiers, and apply data minimisation;
  • pseudonymise, generalise and suppress data, check k-anonymity, and explain why de-identification can fail;
  • name the main sources of bias in data and models, and compute simple fairness measures by group;
  • report results honestly, with their uncertainty and limitations;
  • make an analysis reproducible: seeds, recorded versions, scripted steps, untouched raw data and version control.

Data science is done with data about people, for decisions that affect people: who gets a loan, which neighbourhoods get more inspections, which patients are called for a check-up, which job applicants are shortlisted. The same techniques that find useful patterns can expose private lives, repeat old injustices at scale, or give false confidence in a wrong answer. This chapter treats these risks as part of the technical work, because that is where they are created and where most of them can be prevented. It also covers reproducibility: whether someone else (including you, six months later) can repeat the analysis and get the same result, which is the basis of trust in any finding.

import hashlib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

docs.title: 13.1 Ethics across the workflow
docs.text:
Every stage of the workflow of Chapter 1 has its own ethical questions.

Stage Questions to ask Ask Who benefits from the answer, and who could be harmed? Should this be predicted at all? Get data Was it collected with consent, for a purpose compatible with this one? Do we need all of it? Clean Do our cleaning choices (dropping rows, filling values) affect some groups more than others? Explore Are some groups missing or under-represented? Model Does the model use features that stand in for sensitive characteristics? Evaluate Is it equally accurate for different groups? What happens to people when it is wrong? Communicate Are uncertainty and limitations stated? Could the result be misread or misused?

Table 13.1. Ethical questions at each stage of the workflow.

No checklist settles these questions mechanically. They call for judgement, for knowledge of the setting, and often for the views of the people affected. What a data scientist can always do is notice them, measure what can be measured, and say clearly what was decided and why.

docs.title: 13.2 Privacy
docs.text:
Personal data is any information relating to an identifiable person. Some fields identify a person directly: name, phone number, email address, government ID number. These are direct identifiers. Other fields do not identify anyone alone but can in combination: date of birth, PIN code, gender, occupation. These are quasi-identifiers. In many populations, the combination of full date of birth, gender and postal code is unique for a large share of people, so a table with names removed but those three columns kept may still identify almost everyone in it.

Many countries have data protection laws, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Their details differ and are a matter for legal advice, but they share principles that are good practice everywhere:

  • Purpose limitation: collect data for a stated purpose and do not reuse it for unrelated purposes without a proper basis.
  • Data minimisation: collect and keep only what the purpose needs.
  • Consent and transparency: people should know what is collected about them and why.
  • Security: protect data against unauthorised access; restrict who can see identifying fields.
  • Retention limits: delete data when it is no longer needed.

Key idea

The safest personal data is data you never collected. Before asking how to protect a column, ask whether the analysis needs it at all.

docs.title: De-identification techniques
docs.text:
When personal data must be used, several techniques reduce the risk. A small table of (fictional) patient records shows them:

patients = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["A. Rao", "B. Singh", "C. Das", "D. Iyer", "E. Khan", "F. Roy", "G. Paul", "H. Nair"],
    "phone": ["98100 11111", "98100 22222", "98100 33333", "98100 44444",
              "98100 55555", "98100 66666", "98100 77777", "98100 88888"],
    "age": [34, 36, 52, 57, 33, 55, 38, 51],
    "pin": ["411001", "411002", "560001", "560002", "411003", "560003", "411004", "560004"],
    "condition": ["asthma", "diabetes", "diabetes", "hypertension", "asthma", "diabetes", "asthma", "hypertension"],
})
print(patients)

       name        phone  age     pin     condition
0    A. Rao  98100 11111   34  411001        asthma
1  B. Singh  98100 22222   36  411002      diabetes
2    C. Das  98100 33333   52  560001      diabetes
3   D. Iyer  98100 44444   57  560002  hypertension
4   E. Khan  98100 55555   33  411003        asthma
5    F. Roy  98100 66666   55  560003      diabetes
6   G. Paul  98100 77777   38  411004        asthma
7   H. Nair  98100 88888   51  560004  hypertension

Removal. Drop direct identifiers that the analysis does not need, such as names and phone numbers.

Pseudonymisation. Replace an identifier with a code, so that records of the same person can still be linked (across visits, say) without revealing who it is. A cryptographic hash of the identifier combined with a secret value (a salt, or better a key) gives a stable code; without the secret, the code cannot be reversed by trying all possible phone numbers.

SECRET = "replace-with-a-long-random-secret-kept-out-of-the-code"

def pseudonym(value, secret=SECRET):
    return hashlib.sha256((secret + value).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]

deid = patients.assign(pid=patients["phone"].map(pseudonym)).drop(columns=["name", "phone"])
print(deid[["pid", "age", "pin", "condition"]].head(3))

            pid  age     pin condition
0  251d1fd16c70   34  411001    asthma
1  0a169f24a0a3   36  411002  diabetes
2  7a38048e3edd   52  560001  diabetes

Caution: pseudonymised data is still personal data

A pseudonym can be linked back to the person by anyone who holds the secret, and the remaining columns may identify people anyway. Hashing a phone number without a secret is especially weak: there are only so many phone numbers, and an attacker can hash them all and look up the codes. Keep the secret separate from the data, and treat pseudonymised data with nearly the same care as the original.

Generalisation. Make quasi-identifiers coarser: exact age becomes an age band, a six-digit PIN code becomes its first three digits (a wider area), a date of birth becomes a year.

deid["age_band"] = pd.cut(deid["age"], bins=[30, 40, 50, 60], right=False, labels=["30-39", "40-49", "50-59"])
deid["area"] = deid["pin"].str[:3]
released = deid[["pid", "age_band", "area", "condition"]]
print(released)

            pid age_band area     condition
0  251d1fd16c70    30-39  411        asthma
1  0a169f24a0a3    30-39  411      diabetes
2  7a38048e3edd    50-59  560      diabetes
3  9a9500beea8d    50-59  560  hypertension
4  b23f216cd50c    30-39  411        asthma
5  7260b72d69ad    50-59  560      diabetes
6  37950db4bce6    30-39  411        asthma
7  3e66d62ddec6    50-59  560  hypertension

docs.title: k-anonymity
docs.text:
A table is k-anonymous (with respect to a set of quasi-identifiers) if every combination of their values that appears is shared by at least \(k\) records. Then any one person is indistinguishable from at least \(k - 1\) others on those fields. Checking it is a groupby:

def k_anonymity(df, quasi):
    return int(df.groupby(quasi, observed=True).size().min())

print("original (age, pin):     k =", k_anonymity(deid, ["age", "pin"]))
print("generalised (band, area): k =", k_anonymity(released, ["age_band", "area"]))
print(released.groupby(["age_band", "area"], observed=True)["condition"].agg(list))

original (age, pin):     k = 1
generalised (band, area): k = 4
age_band  area
30-39     411                   [asthma, diabetes, asthma, asthma]
50-59     560     [diabetes, hypertension, diabetes, hypertension]
Name: condition, dtype: object

In the original table every person is unique on age and PIN code (\(k = 1\)). After generalisation every combination is shared by four people (\(k = 4\)). But look at the groups' conditions: if everyone in a group had the same condition, knowing that someone is in the group would reveal their condition even with \(k = 4\). Here each group mixes conditions, but this weakness of k-anonymity is real, and stronger notions (such as requiring diverse sensitive values within each group, or the mathematical framework of differential privacy, which adds carefully calibrated noise to published results) exist for that reason.

Suppressing small counts. Published tables of counts leak information when cells are small: "1 patient aged 50–59 in area 411 has hypertension" identifies someone to anyone who knows them. A common rule is to suppress or round cells below a threshold before publication.

docs.title: Re-identification
docs.text: De-identified datasets have repeatedly been re-identified by linking them with other data that contains names together with the same quasi-identifiers (public records, social media, other leaked datasets). The lesson is general: whether a dataset identifies people depends not only on what it contains but on what else exists. Release as little detail as the purpose allows, and prefer sharing aggregates to sharing records.

docs.title: 13.3 Bias and fairness
docs.text:
A model learns patterns from data, and if the data reflects unequal treatment or unequal measurement, so will the model. Bias enters in several ways:

  • Sampling bias: the data does not represent the population the model will be used on (a health model trained mostly on one region or age group).
  • Measurement bias: a variable is measured differently, or with different accuracy, for different groups.
  • Historical bias: the data faithfully records past decisions that were themselves unfair (past hiring decisions used as the "correct" labels for a hiring model).
  • Proxy features: a model that is not given a sensitive attribute (gender, caste, religion) can still pick it up through correlated features, such as a PIN code or the name of a college.

docs.title: Measuring fairness by group
docs.text:
The first step is to measure. Here is a simulated lending scenario. Applicants belong to group A or group B. Their true ability to repay is distributed identically in the two groups, but the historical data recorded group B's repayment ability through a noisier and lower-scored "credit history" feature, as can happen when one group has had less access to formal credit. A model is trained on that data and used to approve loans.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
n = 4000
group = rng.choice(["A", "B"], n)
ability = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                                   # same distribution in both groups
income = ability * 0.8 + rng.normal(0, 0.6, n)
history = np.where(group == "A", ability + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n),
                   ability - 0.7 + rng.normal(0, 1.0, n))       # biased, noisier for B
repaid = (ability + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n) > -0.3).astype(int)
loans = pd.DataFrame({"group": group, "income": income, "history": history, "repaid": repaid})

X = loans[["income", "history"]]                                 # the group itself is NOT a feature
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, g_tr, g_te = train_test_split(X, loans["repaid"], loans["group"],
                                                      test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)
approve = model.predict(X_te)

report = pd.DataFrame({"group": g_te.values, "repaid": y_te.values, "approved": approve})
def rates(d):
    good = d["repaid"] == 1
    return pd.Series({
        "applicants": len(d),
        "actual repay rate": d["repaid"].mean(),
        "approval rate": d["approved"].mean(),
        "approved | would repay": d.loc[good, "approved"].mean(),       # true positive rate
        "approved | would default": d.loc[~good, "approved"].mean(),    # false positive rate
    })
fair = report.groupby("group")[["repaid", "approved"]].apply(rates).round(3)
print(fair.T)

group                            A        B
applicants                1032.000  968.000
actual repay rate            0.610    0.610
approval rate                0.694    0.596
approved | would repay       0.905    0.810
approved | would default     0.363    0.262

The two groups would repay at the same rate (61%), yet group B is approved noticeably less often, and, more tellingly, among applicants who would repay, a smaller share of group B is approved. The model never saw the group label; the bias came in through the history feature, which measures group B's ability less accurately and systematically lower.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
metrics = ["actual repay rate", "approval rate", "approved | would repay"]
xpos = np.arange(len(metrics))
ax.bar(xpos - 0.2, fair.loc["A", metrics], width=0.4, label="group A")
ax.bar(xpos + 0.2, fair.loc["B", metrics], width=0.4, label="group B")
ax.set_xticks(xpos, ["would repay", "approved", "approved if\nwould repay"])
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("rate")
ax.set_title("Same ability to repay, different treatment")
ax.legend()
fig.savefig("fairness.svg")
Figure 13.1 A model can treat equally able groups differently. A grouped bar chart comparing groups A and B on three rates. The share who would repay is almost the same for both groups. The approval rate is lower for group B, and the approval rate among applicants who would repay is also clearly lower for group B than for group A.

Several fairness criteria are in common use. Demographic parity asks for equal approval rates across groups. Equal opportunity asks for equal true positive rates: those who would repay should be approved at the same rate whatever their group. Equalised odds asks for equal true positive and false positive rates. When the groups' base rates differ, these criteria generally cannot all hold at once, so choosing between them is a value judgement about what fairness means in the setting, not a technical detail.

Caution: removing the sensitive column is not enough

The model above never used the group label and was still unfair, because another feature carried the group's disadvantage. "We don't use gender (or caste, or religion) in the model" is not a demonstration of fairness. Fairness has to be measured, which requires knowing group membership for at least an evaluation sample.

What can be done? Improve the data (measure the disadvantaged group's ability better, collect more representative data); reconsider features that act as proxies; adjust decision thresholds per group to equalise a chosen criterion, where that is lawful and appropriate; and, sometimes, decide that a decision should not be automated at all. Whatever is done, report the group-wise metrics with the model.

docs.title: 13.4 Honest analysis and communication
docs.text:
Ethics also concerns the truthfulness of results. Earlier chapters met the main ways analyses mislead:

  • Charts that distort: bar charts not starting at zero, unequal scales, cherry-picked time windows (Section 6.8).
  • Fishing for significance: running many tests and reporting the ones with \(p < 0.05\); adjusting the analysis until a desired result appears (Section 7.6).
  • Optimistic evaluation: tuning on the test set, leakage, no baseline (Chapter 10).
  • Causal language for associations: "studying causes higher marks" from observational data (Section 6.6).
  • Hiding uncertainty: reporting a single number without an interval, or with false precision.

The remedy is a habit of reporting that a sceptical colleague could check: the question, the data and its limitations, every exclusion and cleaning decision, the methods, the uncertainty, and what the result does not show.

docs.title: 13.5 Reproducibility
docs.text:
An analysis is reproducible if someone else can take the same data and code and obtain the same results. It sounds automatic for computer work, but in practice results are often impossible to recreate: a cell run out of order in a notebook, a file edited by hand, a library that changed its defaults, an unrecorded random seed. Reproducibility is what lets errors be found and results be trusted.

The practices are simple:

  1. Never edit raw data. Keep the original files read-only, and do every cleaning step in code (Section 5.11), so that the path from raw data to result is complete.
  2. Fix random seeds. Pass random_state to scikit-learn and use np.random.default_rng(seed), as this book does everywhere.
  3. Record the environment. Note the versions of Python and of each library; the same code can give different results, or fail, under other versions.
  4. Script the analysis. Put the steps in functions and scripts that run from start to finish. In a notebook, regularly use "restart and run all" to confirm the notebook runs top to bottom and produces what it shows.
  5. Use version control. Keep code (and small data or its description) in a version-control system such as git, so that every result can be tied to the exact code that produced it.
  6. Document decisions. A short text file explaining the data source, each cleaning decision and the reasons for the modelling choices is worth more than any amount of clever code.

Recording versions takes two lines:

import sys, sklearn, matplotlib
print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
print("numpy", np.__version__, "| pandas", pd.__version__,
      "| matplotlib", matplotlib.__version__, "| scikit-learn", sklearn.__version__)

Python 3.12.10
numpy 2.5.3 | pandas 3.0.5 | matplotlib 3.11.2 | scikit-learn 1.9.0

A file listing the exact versions, conventionally requirements.txt, lets others install the same environment with pip install -r requirements.txt:

numpy==2.5.3
pandas==3.0.5
matplotlib==3.11.2
scikit-learn==1.9.0

A seed makes a random result repeatable, which is easy to check:

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

def fit_score(seed):
    m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, random_state=seed).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    return round(m.score(X_te, y_te), 4)

print(fit_score(1), fit_score(1), fit_score(2))

0.7565 0.7565 0.7535

The same seed gives exactly the same score; a different seed gives a slightly different one. That difference is also informative: if a result changes materially with the seed, it was never robust, and reporting the spread over several seeds is more honest than reporting the best one.

Note: reproducible is not the same as correct

A reproducible analysis can still be wrong, but its errors can be found, because anyone can rerun it, inspect each step and change one thing at a time. An irreproducible analysis cannot even be checked.

docs.title: 13.6 A checklist for responsible projects
docs.text:
Example 13.1: Questions to answer before a model is used

  • Purpose: What decision will this support, and who is affected by it?
  • Data: Where did the data come from, with what consent, and which groups are missing or under-represented?
  • Privacy: Which personal fields are used, and are they all necessary? How are they protected, and when will they be deleted?
  • Performance: How does the model compare with a baseline, measured without leakage, with uncertainty?
  • Fairness: Are error rates similar across relevant groups? If not, what has been done, and is the remaining difference acceptable?
  • Failure: What happens to a person when the model is wrong, and can they challenge the decision?
  • Reproducibility: Can the result be recreated from raw data with recorded code, seeds and versions?
  • Monitoring: Who checks the model after deployment, and how often?

docs.title: 13.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Ethical questions arise at every stage of the workflow; notice them, measure what can be measured, and document decisions.
  • Direct identifiers name people; quasi-identifiers identify them in combination. Collect only what the purpose needs.
  • Remove, pseudonymise (keyed hashes, secret kept separate), generalise and suppress; check k-anonymity with a groupby. De-identified data can be re-identified by linkage, and pseudonymised data is still personal data.
  • Bias enters through sampling, measurement, historical labels and proxy features. Removing a sensitive column does not remove bias.
  • Measure fairness by group: approval rates (demographic parity), true positive rates (equal opportunity), and false positive rates (equalised odds). Choosing a criterion is a value judgement.
  • Report honestly: undistorted charts, no fishing, no leakage, no causal claims from associations, and uncertainty stated.
  • Reproducibility: raw data untouched, seeds fixed, versions recorded, steps scripted, code under version control, decisions documented.

docs.title: 13.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each field as a direct identifier, a quasi-identifier, or neither: (a) email address; (b) year of birth; (c) blood pressure reading; (d) PIN code; (e) passport number; (f) occupation.

Answer

Direct identifiers: (a) email address, (e) passport number. Quasi-identifiers: (b) year of birth, (d) PIN code, (f) occupation, which can identify people in combination. (c) A blood pressure reading is a sensitive attribute but not normally an identifier (though in a small dataset an unusual value combined with other fields could help identify someone).

Exercise 2

Why is hashlib.sha256(phone.encode()).hexdigest() a weak way to pseudonymise ten-digit phone numbers? How does the chapter's pseudonym function improve on it?

Answer

There are at most \(10^{10}\) ten-digit numbers, so an attacker can hash every possible number and build a lookup table from codes back to numbers; an unsalted hash therefore hides nothing. Adding a long secret value before hashing means the attacker would also need the secret to build the table. The secret must be kept separate from the data, since anyone holding it can still re-identify.

Exercise 3

For the table below, what is the k-anonymity with respect to (age_band, area)? Generalise it to make \(k \ge 2\).

t = pd.DataFrame({"age_band": ["20-29", "20-29", "30-39", "30-39", "30-39"],
                  "area": ["411", "411", "411", "560", "560"]})
print(k_anonymity(t, ["age_band", "area"]))

1
Answer

\(k = 1\): the combination (30-39, 411) occurs once. One fix is to generalise the area for that band, for example replacing all areas by a coarser region, or merging the age bands to "20-39":

t2 = t.assign(age_band="20-39")
print(k_anonymity(t2, ["age_band", "area"]))

2

Now the groups are (20-39, 411) with 3 records and (20-39, 560) with 2, so \(k = 2\). Each generalisation loses detail; the art is to lose as little as needed.

Exercise 4

In the lending example, compute the false positive rate (approval among applicants who would default) for each group from fair, and say which fairness criterion the comparison relates to.

Answer 
print(fair["approved | would default"])

group
A    0.363
B    0.262
Name: approved | would default, dtype: float64

This is the false positive rate per group. Comparing false positive rates (together with true positive rates) is the equalised odds criterion; equal true positive rates alone is equal opportunity.

Exercise 5

A colleague's notebook gives a different answer each time it is run from the top. List three likely causes.

Answer

For example: a random step (a train/test split, a shuffle, a random forest, k-means initialisation) without a fixed seed; cells that depend on state created by cells run earlier out of order, or on variables that have since been deleted; data read from a file or a source that changes between runs (a live database, a file someone edits). Less often: library versions that differ between machines.

Exercise 6

A city wants to use a model to decide where to send food-safety inspectors, trained on past inspection results. Name one way historical bias could enter, and one check you would make.

Answer

Past inspections may have been concentrated in certain neighbourhoods, so violations were found more often there simply because more inspections took place; a model trained on those results would send inspectors back to the same places, reinforcing the pattern. A check: compare inspection rates and violation rates per inspection across neighbourhoods, and evaluate the model on a sample of randomly chosen inspections, which are free of the old targeting.

docs.title: 13.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 13

Exercise 1

Which of these is a quasi-identifier?

  1. full name
  2. passport number
  3. date of birth
  4. a random study number
Answer

date of birth

Exercise 2

A table is 3-anonymous on its quasi-identifiers if

  1. it has 3 columns
  2. every combination of quasi-identifier values appears at least 3 times
  3. 3 identifiers were removed
  4. 3 people can see it
Answer

every combination of quasi-identifier values appears at least 3 times

Exercise 3

Removing the sensitive attribute from a model's features

  1. guarantees fairness
  2. does not by itself guarantee fairness
  3. is illegal
  4. always lowers accuracy
Answer

does not by itself guarantee fairness

Exercise 4

Equal opportunity asks for equal

  1. approval rates
  2. true positive rates
  3. accuracy
  4. group sizes
Answer

true positive rates

Exercise 5

Which practice most directly makes a random result repeatable?

  1. using more data
  2. fixing the random seed
  3. using a notebook
  4. removing outliers
Answer

fixing the random seed

Exercise 6

What is the conventional name of the file that lists a Python project's exact package versions?

Answer

requirements.txt

Exercise 7

Pseudonymised data is

  1. anonymous and free to share
  2. still personal data
  3. always encrypted
  4. useless for analysis
Answer

still personal data
