docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The terms of the book, with the chapter where each is explained

docs.title: A–C
docs.text: Accuracy The fraction of a classifier's predictions that are correct. Misleading when one class is much more common than the other (Chapter 9). Agglomerative clustering Hierarchical clustering that starts with every example as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters, according to a linkage rule (Chapter 11). Aggregation Combining many values into one, such as a sum, mean, count or maximum (Chapters 2, 3 and 5). Alignment pandas' matching of values by index label, rather than by position, when two Series or DataFrames are combined (Chapter 4). AUC Area under the ROC curve: the probability that a classifier scores a randomly chosen positive example above a randomly chosen negative one; 0.5 is random guessing, 1 is perfect (Chapter 10). Axis A dimension of an array. In an aggregation, the axis named is the one that disappears: axis=0 gives one result per column (Chapter 3). In matplotlib, an Axes object is one plot within a figure (Chapter 6). Bag of words A representation of a document by the counts of the words it contains, ignoring their order (Chapter 12). Baseline A trivial model, such as predicting the mean or the most common class, against which real models are compared (Chapters 8 and 9). Bias (statistical) A systematic difference between an estimate and the true value. In modelling, the error that comes from a model too simple to capture the pattern (underfitting) (Chapters 7 and 8). Bias (in data) Systematic distortion in how data was sampled, measured or labelled, which a model trained on it can reproduce (Chapter 13). Binning Turning a numerical variable into ordered categories, with pd.cut or pd.qcut (Chapter 5). Bootstrap Estimating the sampling variation of a statistic by recomputing it on many resamples drawn with replacement from the data (Chapter 7). Box plot A chart of a distribution showing the median, the quartiles, whiskers, and points beyond 1.5 interquartile ranges as possible outliers (Chapter 6). Broadcasting NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes by stretching dimensions of length 1 (Chapter 3). Categorical variable A variable whose values are categories: nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered) (Chapter 1). Central limit theorem The result that the mean of many independent observations is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the population (Chapter 7). Centroid The mean of the examples in a cluster; k-means represents each cluster by its centroid (Chapter 11). Chained assignment Selecting from a DataFrame twice and assigning to the result, as in df[mask]["col"] = value; it never changes the original under copy-on-write (Chapter 4). Classification Supervised learning in which the target is a category (Chapter 9). Clustering Grouping examples so that those in a group are more similar to each other than to those in other groups, without using labels (Chapter 11). Coefficient of determination (\(R^2\)) One minus the ratio of a model's squared error to that of predicting the mean; 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the mean (Chapter 8). Confidence interval A range of plausible values for a parameter, computed by a method that captures the true value in a stated share (such as 95%) of samples (Chapter 7). Confusion matrix A table counting true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives (Chapter 9). Copy-on-write pandas' rule (always on from version 3) that a selection behaves as an independent copy, so changing it never changes the original table (Chapter 4). Correlation Pearson's \(r\), a measure from \(-1\) to \(1\) of the strength of a straight-line relationship between two numerical variables (Chapter 6). Cosine similarity The cosine of the angle between two vectors; used to compare documents represented as TF-IDF vectors (Chapter 12). Cross-validation Estimating performance by training on part of the data and validating on the rest, repeatedly, so that every example is used for validation once (Chapter 10). CSV Comma-separated values: plain text with one record per line and fields separated by commas (Chapters 2 and 4).

docs.title: D–H
docs.text: Data leakage The use, during training or evaluation, of information that would not be available when the model is used, making the evaluation falsely optimistic (Chapter 10). Data minimisation The principle of collecting and keeping only the personal data that a purpose needs (Chapter 13). DataFrame pandas' table: a set of Series (columns) sharing one index (Chapter 4). Decision boundary The border between the regions of feature space that a classifier assigns to different classes (Chapter 9). Decision tree A model that predicts by a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, grown by choosing splits that make groups purer (Chapter 9). Dendrogram A tree diagram showing the order and distances at which hierarchical clustering merged clusters (Chapter 11). Distribution The pattern of how often each value of a variable occurs; for a random variable, the probabilities of its values (Chapters 6 and 7). dtype The type of the values in a NumPy array or a pandas column, such as int64, float64 or str (Chapters 3 and 4). Expectation The long-run average value of a random variable, also called its mean (Chapter 7). Exploratory data analysis (EDA) Getting to know a dataset through summaries and charts before modelling it (Chapter 6). F1 score The harmonic mean of precision and recall (Chapter 9). Feature An input variable used by a model to make predictions (Chapter 8). Feature importance A measure of how much a model relies on each feature; see permutation importance (Chapters 9 and 14). Gini impurity \(1 - \sum_c p_c^2\), a measure of how mixed the classes in a group are; decision trees choose splits that reduce it (Chapter 9). Gradient boosting An ensemble method that adds decision trees one after another, each fitted to correct the errors of those before (Chapter 14). Grid search Trying every combination in a grid of hyperparameter values and keeping the one with the best cross-validated score (Chapter 10). Groupby pandas' split-apply-combine operation: split rows into groups by a key, apply a function to each, and combine the results (Chapter 5). Histogram A chart of a numerical variable's distribution, with bars counting the values in each interval (bin) (Chapter 6). Hyperparameter A setting chosen before training, such as \(k\) in k-NN or the depth of a tree, rather than learned from the data (Chapters 8 to 10). Hypothesis test A procedure for judging whether data is consistent with a null hypothesis, usually summarised by a p-value (Chapter 7).

docs.title: I–O
docs.text: Imputation Filling in missing values, for example with the median of a column (Chapters 5 and 14). Index The labels of the rows of a pandas Series or DataFrame (Chapter 4). Inertia The sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster's centroid, which k-means minimises (Chapter 11). Interquartile range (IQR) The distance between the first and third quartiles; the box of a box plot (Chapters 5 and 6). k-anonymity The property that every combination of quasi-identifier values in a table is shared by at least \(k\) records (Chapter 13). k-fold cross-validation Cross-validation with the data divided into \(k\) folds, each used once for validation (Chapter 10). k-means A clustering algorithm that alternates assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to the mean of their points (Chapter 11). k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) A classifier that predicts by a majority vote of the \(k\) closest training examples (Chapter 9). Lag A copy of a time series shifted so that each time point sees an earlier value; created with shift (Chapter 12). Lasso Linear regression with a penalty on the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients, which can set some coefficients exactly to zero (Chapter 8). Least squares Fitting a model by minimising the sum of squared residuals (Chapter 8). Logistic regression A classification model that passes a linear combination of the features through the sigmoid function to give a probability (Chapter 9). Mean absolute error (MAE) The average absolute difference between predictions and true values (Chapter 8). Median The middle value of sorted data; half the values lie below it (Chapters 1 and 6). Missing value A value that was not recorded, shown by pandas as NaN, NaT or <NA> (Chapters 3 and 5). Normal distribution The symmetric bell-shaped distribution fixed by its mean and standard deviation (Chapter 7). Null hypothesis In a hypothesis test, the "no effect" or "no difference" position that the test assesses (Chapter 7). One-hot encoding Representing a categorical variable by one 0/1 column per category (Chapter 8). Outlier A value far from the rest of the data, which may be genuine or an error (Chapters 5 and 6). Overfitting Fitting the noise of the training data as well as the pattern, so that performance on new data suffers (Chapter 8).

docs.title: P–S
docs.text: p-value The probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed (Chapter 7). Permutation importance The increase in a model's error when one feature's values are randomly shuffled (Chapter 14). Permutation test A hypothesis test that compares an observed statistic with its values after many random reshufflings of the group labels (Chapter 7). Pipeline A chain of preprocessing steps and a model that is fitted and used as one estimator, so that every step learns from training data only (Chapters 8 to 10). Population The whole set of cases about which conclusions are wanted; a sample is drawn from it (Chapter 7). Power The probability that a hypothesis test detects a real effect of a given size (Chapter 7). Precision Of the examples predicted positive, the fraction that truly are positive: \(TP/(TP + FP)\) (Chapter 9). Principal component analysis (PCA) A method that finds orthogonal directions of greatest variance in the data, used to reduce the number of dimensions (Chapter 11). Pseudonymisation Replacing an identifier with a code that cannot be traced back without separately held information, such as a secret key (Chapter 13). Quasi-identifier A field, such as date of birth or postal code, that does not identify a person alone but can in combination with others (Chapter 13). Random forest An ensemble of decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample with random subsets of features, whose predictions are averaged or voted (Chapter 9). Recall Of the truly positive examples, the fraction predicted positive: \(TP/(TP + FN)\); also called sensitivity or the true positive rate (Chapter 9). Regression Supervised learning in which the target is a number (Chapter 8). Regularisation Adding a penalty on the size of a model's coefficients to the loss, to reduce overfitting (Chapter 8). Reproducibility The property that the same data and code give the same results when the analysis is rerun by anyone (Chapter 13). Resampling (time series) Changing the frequency of a time series, for example from daily to monthly, with resample (Chapter 12). Residual The difference between a true value and a model's prediction, \(y - \hat{y}\) (Chapter 8). Ridge regression Linear regression with a penalty on the sum of squared coefficients (Chapter 8). ROC curve A plot of the true positive rate against the false positive rate over all classification thresholds (Chapter 10). Sampling distribution The distribution of a statistic over all possible samples of a given size (Chapter 7). Seed The starting value of a pseudo-random number generator; fixing it makes random results repeatable (Chapters 2, 3 and 13). Series pandas' one-dimensional labelled array: values plus an index (Chapter 4). Sigmoid The function \(1/(1 + e^{-z})\), which maps any number to the range 0 to 1 (Chapter 9). Silhouette score The average over all points of \((b - a)/\max(a, b)\), comparing distances within a point's cluster (\(a\)) and to the nearest other cluster (\(b\)) (Chapter 11). Skew Asymmetry of a distribution; a right-skewed distribution has a long tail of large values (Chapter 6). Standard deviation The square root of the variance; a measure of spread in the units of the data (Chapters 3 and 7). Standard error The standard deviation of a statistic's sampling distribution; for a mean, \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) (Chapter 7). Standardisation Rescaling a variable to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation (Chapters 3, 8 and 9). Stratified split A split or set of folds that keeps the same proportion of each class in every part (Chapters 9 and 10). Supervised learning Learning to predict a target from examples where the target is known (Chapter 8).

docs.title: T–Z
docs.text: Target The variable a model predicts, also called the label or response (Chapter 8). Test set Data held back and used once, at the end, to estimate how a final model performs on new data (Chapters 8 and 10). TF-IDF Term frequency–inverse document frequency: word counts reweighted so that words common to many documents count less (Chapter 12). Threshold The predicted probability above which a classifier predicts the positive class; 0.5 by default (Chapter 9). Tidy data A table with one variable per column and one observation per row (Chapter 1). Time series Measurements of a quantity taken in time order (Chapters 6 and 12). Tokenisation Splitting text into units, usually words, called tokens (Chapter 12). Training set The data used to fit a model's parameters (Chapter 8). Type I error Rejecting a true null hypothesis: a false positive (Chapter 7). Type II error Failing to reject a false null hypothesis: a missed effect (Chapter 7). Underfitting Using a model too simple to capture the pattern in the data, so that it does poorly on both training and new data (Chapter 8). Unsupervised learning Finding structure in data without a target, as in clustering and dimensionality reduction (Chapter 11). Validation set Data used to make choices about a model, such as its hyperparameters, separate from the test set (Chapter 10). Variance (of a random variable) The average squared distance of a random variable from its mean (Chapter 7). Variance (in modelling) The error that comes from a model's sensitivity to the particular training sample; high in overfitted models (Chapter 8). Vectorisation Writing operations on whole arrays or columns at once instead of looping over elements (Chapter 3). z-score The number of standard deviations by which a value lies above or below the mean: \((x - \mu)/\sigma\) (Chapter 7).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Model Evaluation and Cross-Validation
docs.text:
Estimating honestly how well a model will do on data it has never seen

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why a model must be judged on data not used to build it, and what the test set is for;
  • use training, validation and test sets correctly;
  • estimate performance with k-fold cross-validation and report its mean and spread;
  • tune hyperparameters with a grid search inside cross-validation;
  • recognise and prevent data leakage, including leakage through preprocessing, time and groups;
  • read a ROC curve and its AUC, and a precision–recall curve;
  • compare models fairly and report results with their uncertainty.

A model is useful only if it works on cases it has not seen: next month's customers, tomorrow's transactions, the patient who walks in today. Its performance on the data it was trained on says little about that, because a flexible model can memorise its training data (Chapters 8 and 9). This chapter is about estimating generalisation performance honestly. It is the stage of the workflow where most of the self-deception in data science happens, usually by accident, and the habits it teaches matter more than any single algorithm.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

We reuse the churn data of Chapter 9, generated by the same code, wrapped in a function so that it can be called again:

def make_churn(n=1000, seed=10):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    tenure = rng.integers(1, 72, n)
    charge = rng.uniform(200, 1200, n).round(0)
    calls = rng.poisson(1.5, n)
    contract = rng.choice(["monthly", "yearly"], n, p=[0.55, 0.45])
    logit = (-2.5 - 0.05 * tenure + 0.0025 * charge + 0.45 * calls
             + np.where(contract == "monthly", 1.0, -0.8))
    churn = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    X = pd.DataFrame({"tenure": tenure, "charge": charge, "calls": calls,
                      "monthly": (contract == "monthly").astype(int)})
    return X, pd.Series(churn, name="churn")

X, y = make_churn()
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1, stratify=y)
print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape, round(y.mean(), 3))

(800, 4) (200, 4) 0.244

docs.title: 10.1 Three roles for data
docs.text:
Data in a modelling project plays three distinct roles.

  • The training set is used to fit the model's parameters (coefficients, tree splits).
  • The validation set is used to make choices: which model, which features, which hyperparameters (\(k\) in k-NN, depth of a tree, \(\alpha\) in ridge).
  • The test set is used once, at the end, to estimate how the final chosen model will perform on new data.

Why not make the choices on the test set? Because every choice made by looking at a dataset adapts the model to that dataset. Try twenty models and keep the one with the best test score, and that score is the maximum of twenty noisy numbers, which is optimistic. The test set must be kept out of every decision so that its score remains an honest estimate. Think of it as an exam paper: if you have seen the questions while studying, your mark no longer measures what you know.

Key idea

Any data used to make a decision about the model, even just to choose between two options, is no longer a fair test. Hold the test set back until all decisions are made, and look at it once.

A single validation set is wasteful when data is limited, and its score is noisy: it depends on which examples happened to land in it. Cross-validation solves both problems.

docs.title: 10.2 k-fold cross-validation
docs.text:
In k-fold cross-validation the training data is divided into \(k\) equal parts, called folds. The model is trained \(k\) times, each time on \(k - 1\) folds, and scored on the remaining fold. Every example is used for validation exactly once, and the \(k\) scores are averaged (Figure 10.1). Five or ten folds are the usual choices.

Figure 10.1 A test set and five-fold cross-validation. The data is first split into a training part (80%) and a test part (20%) that is set aside. The training part is divided into five folds. In each of five rounds a different fold is used for validation and the other four for training, giving five scores, s1 to s5, whose mean is the cross-validated score. 
logreg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
scores = cross_val_score(logreg, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="accuracy")
print(scores.round(3))
print(f"mean {scores.mean():.3f}, sd {scores.std():.3f}")

[0.819 0.856 0.825 0.819 0.831]
mean 0.830, sd 0.014

The five scores differ by several percentage points, which shows how much a single split could have misled us. Report both the mean and the spread. For classification, scikit-learn's cv=5 uses stratified folds, each with the same proportion of each class as the whole, which keeps the folds comparable when one class is rare.

The scoring argument chooses the metric: "accuracy", "f1", "precision", "recall", "roc_auc" for classifiers; "r2", "neg_mean_absolute_error", "neg_root_mean_squared_error" for regressors (negated so that larger is always better). cross_validate computes several at once:

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

res = cross_validate(logreg, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring=["accuracy", "f1", "roc_auc"])
print(pd.DataFrame(res).drop(columns=["fit_time", "score_time"]).agg(["mean", "std"]).round(3))

      test_accuracy  test_f1  test_roc_auc
mean          0.830    0.600         0.859
std           0.016    0.055         0.019

docs.title: Comparing models
docs.text:
Cross-validation puts several candidate models on the same footing. Using the same folds for each (by passing the same cv object) makes the comparison fairer still.

from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
candidates = {
    "baseline": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "logistic": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()),
    "k-NN (k=25)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(25)),
    "tree (depth 3)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0),
    "forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0),
}
for name, model in candidates.items():
    s = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
    print(f"{name:>15}: AUC {s.mean():.3f} +/- {s.std():.3f}")

       baseline: AUC 0.500 +/- 0.000
       logistic: AUC 0.854 +/- 0.004
    k-NN (k=25): AUC 0.839 +/- 0.007
 tree (depth 3): AUC 0.763 +/- 0.019
         forest: AUC 0.828 +/- 0.019

The AUC (Section 10.5) of the baseline is exactly 0.5: it ranks every customer the same. Logistic regression comes out on top here, which is no surprise since the data was generated by a logistic rule; on real data the ranking could be different, which is exactly why we compare. The gaps between the top three are only one to three hundredths of AUC, comparable to the fold-to-fold spread of the forest, so we should not read too much into their exact order. The shallow tree is clearly behind.

docs.title: 10.3 Tuning hyperparameters
docs.text:
Hyperparameters are settings chosen before training: \(k\) for k-NN, the depth of a tree, the penalty \(C\) of logistic regression. The standard way to choose them is to try a grid of values and keep the one with the best cross-validated score. GridSearchCV does exactly this, and then refits the best setting on the whole training set.

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier())
grid = GridSearchCV(knn, param_grid={"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": [1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 41, 61, 91]},
                    cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("best k:", grid.best_params_, "CV AUC", round(grid.best_score_, 3))
results = pd.DataFrame(grid.cv_results_)[["param_kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors", "mean_test_score", "std_test_score"]]
print(results.round(3).to_string(index=False))

best k: {'kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors': 25} CV AUC 0.839
 param_kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors  mean_test_score  std_test_score
                                       1            0.669           0.039
                                       3            0.751           0.020
                                       5            0.793           0.013
                                       9            0.810           0.021
                                      15            0.823           0.011
                                      25            0.839           0.007
                                      41            0.836           0.016
                                      61            0.832           0.019
                                      91            0.834           0.024

Parameters of a step inside a pipeline are named step__parameter, with two underscores; make_pipeline names each step after its class in lower case.

A plot of the score against the hyperparameter, a validation curve, shows the trade-off between underfitting and overfitting. Here it is for the depth of a decision tree, with the training score for comparison:

from sklearn.model_selection import validation_curve

depths = np.arange(1, 16)
train_sc, val_sc = validation_curve(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), X_train, y_train,
                                    param_name="max_depth", param_range=depths, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(depths, train_sc.mean(axis=1), marker="o", label="training score")
ax.plot(depths, val_sc.mean(axis=1), marker="o", label="cross-validated score")
ax.set_xlabel("maximum depth of the tree")
ax.set_ylabel("ROC AUC")
ax.set_title("Validation curve for a decision tree")
ax.legend()
fig.savefig("validation-curve.svg")
print("best depth:", depths[val_sc.mean(axis=1).argmax()])

best depth: 5
Figure 10.2 Underfitting on the left, overfitting on the right. A validation curve for a decision tree. The training score rises steadily with depth towards 1. The cross-validated score rises at first, peaks at a small depth, and then falls as the tree grows deeper, while the gap between the two curves widens.

On the left both scores are low: shallow trees underfit. On the right the training score keeps climbing while the validation score falls: deep trees overfit. The best depth lies where the validation score peaks.

Note: the best CV score is itself optimistic

The winning setting of a grid search was selected because its cross-validated score was highest, so that score is slightly optimistic, for the same reason as choosing on the test set. With a held-out test set this does not matter: the final test score is unbiased. When the data is too small for a test set, nested cross-validation (an outer cross-validation loop around the whole grid search) gives an honest estimate.

docs.title: 10.4 Data leakage
docs.text: Data leakage means that information which would not be available at prediction time finds its way into training or evaluation. It produces models that look excellent in evaluation and fail in use. It takes several forms.

docs.title: Leakage through preprocessing
docs.text:
Any step that learns from data (a scaler's means, an imputer's medians, a choice of features) must learn from the training folds only. Done on the whole dataset before splitting, it lets the validation data influence training. With a mild step like scaling the effect is small; with feature selection it can be dramatic. Here is a stark demonstration on pure noise: 100 examples, 5,000 random features, and random labels, so that no model can truly do better than 50%.

from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X_noise = rng.normal(size=(100, 5000))
y_noise = rng.integers(0, 2, 100)

# WRONG: choose the 20 "best" features using all the data, then cross-validate
selected = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(X_noise, y_noise).get_support()
wrong = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_noise[:, selected], y_noise, cv=5)

# RIGHT: feature selection inside the pipeline, refitted within each training fold
right = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20), LogisticRegression()),
                        X_noise, y_noise, cv=5)
print(f"selection outside CV: accuracy {wrong.mean():.2f}")
print(f"selection inside CV:  accuracy {right.mean():.2f}")

selection outside CV: accuracy 0.85
selection inside CV:  accuracy 0.48

Selecting features on all the data finds the 20 noise features that happen to line up with the labels including the validation examples, so cross-validation then reports an accuracy far above chance on data with no signal at all. Inside the pipeline, the selection is made on each training fold alone and the accuracy falls back to about 50%, the truth.

Caution: put every learned step inside the pipeline

Scaling, imputing missing values, encoding categories, selecting features, reducing dimensions: if a step learns anything from the data, put it in a Pipeline with the model and cross-validate the whole pipeline. Then each fold repeats the full procedure on its own training data, exactly as will happen when the model is used.

docs.title: Target leakage
docs.text: A feature can leak the answer. In a churn model, a column "cancellation_reason" is filled in only for customers who have already left; in a model to predict hospital readmission, "number of days in hospital this year" may include the readmission itself. Such features predict superbly in historical data and are useless, or impossible to obtain, at prediction time. The defence is to ask of every feature: would I know this value at the moment I need to make the prediction?

docs.title: Leakage through time and groups
docs.text:
When data has an order in time, random splits let the model train on the future and predict the past. A forecast must be evaluated on periods that come after its training data; scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit makes folds that respect order (Chapter 12).

When several rows belong to the same unit (several visits by one patient, several photos of one person, several readings from one machine), a random split puts rows of the same unit in both training and validation, and the model is rewarded for recognising the unit rather than for generalising to new ones. GroupKFold keeps all rows of a group in the same fold.

from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold

patients = np.repeat(np.arange(10), 3)      # 10 patients, 3 visits each
gkf = GroupKFold(n_splits=5)
for i, (tr, va) in enumerate(gkf.split(np.zeros(30), groups=patients)):
    print(f"fold {i}: validation patients {sorted(set(patients[va].tolist()))}")

fold 0: validation patients [4, 9]
fold 1: validation patients [3, 8]
fold 2: validation patients [2, 7]
fold 3: validation patients [1, 6]
fold 4: validation patients [0, 5]

docs.title: 10.5 ROC curves, AUC and precision–recall curves
docs.text:
Chapter 9 showed that moving the classification threshold trades precision against recall. Two curves show the whole trade-off at once, for every threshold.

The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) plots the true positive rate (recall, \(TP/(TP+FN)\)) against the false positive rate (\(FP/(FP+TN)\)) as the threshold moves from 1 down to 0. A model that ranks perfectly goes straight up to the top-left corner; a model that guesses at random follows the diagonal. The area under the curve (AUC) summarises it in one number: 1 is perfect, 0.5 is random. AUC has a useful interpretation: it is the probability that the model gives a randomly chosen positive example a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one.

The precision–recall curve plots precision against recall over all thresholds. It is more informative than the ROC curve when the positive class is rare, because the false positive rate can look tiny even when false positives far outnumber true positives.

from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score, precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score

final = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(X_train, y_train)
scores_test = final.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, scores_test)
prec, rec, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, scores_test)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
axes[0].plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"logistic (AUC = {roc_auc_score(y_test, scores_test):.3f})")
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="gray", label="random guessing")
axes[0].set_xlabel("false positive rate")
axes[0].set_ylabel("true positive rate (recall)")
axes[0].set_title("ROC curve")
axes[0].legend(loc="lower right")
axes[1].plot(rec, prec)
axes[1].axhline(y_test.mean(), linestyle="--", color="gray", label="baseline (share of positives)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("recall")
axes[1].set_ylabel("precision")
axes[1].set_title(f"Precision-recall (AP = {average_precision_score(y_test, scores_test):.3f})")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("roc-pr.svg")
print("test AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y_test, scores_test), 3))

test AUC: 0.877
Figure 10.3 ROC and precision-recall curves on the test set. Left: a ROC curve that rises steeply from the origin and bends towards the top-left corner, well above the dashed diagonal of random guessing. Right: a precision-recall curve that is jagged at low recall, where only a few customers are flagged, and then falls steadily as recall increases, staying above a dashed horizontal baseline at the share of churners, about 0.24.

The test AUC (0.877) is close to the cross-validated estimate of Section 10.2 (0.854); a gap of this size is normal sampling variation for a test set of 200, and agreement of this kind is what to expect when the test set has been kept clean. The average precision (AP) summarises the precision–recall curve; its baseline is the share of positives, not 0.5.

docs.title: 10.6 Reporting results
docs.text:
A good evaluation report says:

  1. What was predicted, and for whom: the target, the population, the period.
  2. How the data was split: random, by time, by group; the sizes; whether the test set was used only once.
  3. The metric and why it suits the problem: accuracy, F1, AUC, MAE, and the costs of the different errors.
  4. The baseline's score, so the reader can judge the gain.
  5. Cross-validated scores with their spread, and the final test score.
  6. Limitations: groups the model does worse for, conditions under which it was not tested, assumptions about the future resembling the past.

Here is the final step for the churn model, carried out once:

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score

base = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = final.predict(X_test)
print(f"test accuracy: model {accuracy_score(y_test, pred):.3f}, baseline {accuracy_score(y_test, base.predict(X_test)):.3f}")
print(f"test F1 (churn class): {f1_score(y_test, pred):.3f}")
print(f"test AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, scores_test):.3f}")

test accuracy: model 0.840, baseline 0.755
test F1 (churn class): 0.610
test AUC: 0.877

Caution: the test score is an estimate too

With 200 test examples, an accuracy of 0.84 has a standard error of about \(\sqrt{0.84 \times 0.16 / 200} \approx 0.026\), so differences of a couple of percentage points between models are within the noise. Report results with sensible precision (two or three digits), not as if the fourth decimal meant something.

docs.title: 10.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Judge models on data not used to build them. Training data fits parameters, validation data (or cross-validation) makes choices, and the test set is used once at the end.
  • k-fold cross-validation trains \(k\) times, each time validating on a different fold; report the mean and spread of the scores. Classification uses stratified folds.
  • Compare candidate models with the same folds, and always include a baseline.
  • Tune hyperparameters with GridSearchCV; a validation curve shows underfitting and overfitting. The best CV score is slightly optimistic; the test set or nested CV corrects that.
  • Leakage makes evaluations falsely optimistic: fit every learned preprocessing step inside a pipeline; drop features unavailable at prediction time; split by time for forecasts and by group when rows share a unit.
  • The ROC curve plots true against false positive rate over all thresholds; AUC is the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative. Precision–recall curves suit rare positive classes.
  • Report the target, the split, the metric, the baseline, CV spread, the test score and the limitations.

docs.title: 10.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A student tunes \(k\) for k-NN by trying 30 values and picking the one with the best score on the test set, then reports that score. What is wrong, and how should it be done?

Answer

The test set has been used to make a choice, so the reported score is the best of 30 noisy estimates and is optimistic. The value of \(k\) should be chosen by cross-validation (or a separate validation set) within the training data, for example with GridSearchCV; the chosen model is then scored once on the untouched test set.

Exercise 2

With 1,000 training examples and 10-fold cross-validation, how many examples is each model trained on, and how many models are fitted in total? How many are fitted by a grid search over 6 values with 5-fold CV (including the final refit)?

Answer

Each of the 10 models is trained on 900 examples and validated on 100. The grid search fits \(6 \times 5 = 30\) models in cross-validation, plus one final refit of the best setting on all the training data: 31 fits.

Exercise 3

Cross-validate a decision tree of depth 4 and a random forest on the churn training data with the folds cv, using F1 as the metric. Which is better, and is the difference larger than the fold-to-fold spread?

Answer 
for name, m in [("tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=0)),
                ("forest", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0))]:
    s = cross_val_score(m, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="f1")
    print(f"{name}: F1 {s.mean():.3f} +/- {s.std():.3f}")

tree: F1 0.567 +/- 0.049
forest: F1 0.536 +/- 0.077

Compare the means with the standard deviations: when the gap between the means is smaller than the spread across folds, the evidence that one is better is weak.

Exercise 4

A model to predict whether a loan will default includes the feature "number of missed payments on this loan". The model's AUC is 0.99. Why should you be suspicious?

Answer

Missed payments on the loan are only known after the loan has been running for a while, and they are part of what default means; at the moment of deciding whether to grant the loan, the value would be zero or unknown. This is target leakage: the feature carries information about the outcome that is not available at prediction time, and it explains the implausibly high AUC.

Exercise 5

A classifier's AUC is 0.80. Explain what this means in terms of pairs of examples.

Answer

If you pick one positive example and one negative example at random, the model gives the positive one a higher predicted score 80% of the time. (Ties count as half.)

Exercise 6

A dataset has 5 X-ray images from each of 200 patients. Why is ordinary k-fold cross-validation inappropriate, and what should be used instead?

Answer

Ordinary k-fold puts images of the same patient in both training and validation folds, so the model can score well by recognising patient-specific features rather than the condition, overestimating its performance on new patients. Use GroupKFold with the patient as the group, so that all images of a patient fall in the same fold.

docs.title: 10.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 10

Exercise 1

The test set should be used

  1. to choose hyperparameters
  2. to choose between models
  3. once at the end to estimate performance
  4. as extra training data
Answer

once at the end to estimate performance

Exercise 2

In 5-fold cross-validation, each example is used for validation

  1. never
  2. exactly once
  3. five times
  4. four times
Answer

exactly once

Exercise 3

What AUC does a model that guesses at random have?

  1. 0
  2. 0.25
  3. 0.5
  4. 1
Answer

0.5

Exercise 4

Selecting features on the whole dataset before cross-validation is an example of

  1. regularisation
  2. data leakage
  3. stratification
  4. underfitting
Answer

Exercise 5

Which splitter keeps all rows of the same patient in one fold?

  1. KFold
  2. StratifiedKFold
  3. GroupKFold
  4. TimeSeriesSplit
Answer

Exercise 6

On a validation curve, a large gap between a high training score and a low validation score indicates

  1. underfitting
  2. overfitting
  3. leakage
  4. a good model
Answer
