  • \(p = 0.049\) and \(p = 0.051\) are practically the same evidence; treating 0.05 as a cliff is a habit, not a law.
  • Multiple testing: run 20 tests on pure noise at \(\alpha = 0.05\) and you expect about one "significant" result. Testing many things and reporting only the significant ones manufactures false discoveries.

docs.title: Testing a relationship between two categorical variables
docs.text:
For two categorical variables, the chi-square test of independence compares the observed counts in a contingency table with the counts expected if the variables were unrelated.

table = pd.DataFrame({"bought": [48, 71], "did not buy": [152, 129]}, index=["email A", "email B"])
print(table)
chi2, p, dof, expected = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(f"chi2 = {chi2:.3f}, dof = {dof}, p = {p:.4f}")
print((table["bought"] / table.sum(axis=1)).round(3))

         bought  did not buy
email A      48          152
email B      71          129
chi2 = 5.790, dof = 1, p = 0.0161
email A    0.240
email B    0.355
dtype: float64

Email B converted 35.5% of its 200 recipients against 24% for email A, and the p-value says a difference this large would be unusual if the emails were equally effective.

docs.title: 7.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Probabilities combine by the complement, addition and multiplication rules; conditional probability restricts to the cases where the condition holds, and \(P(A \mid B) \ne P(B \mid A)\) in general.
  • A distribution gives the probabilities of a random variable's values: binomial and Poisson for counts, uniform and normal for continuous values. scipy.stats gives their pmf/pdf, cdf, ppf and random samples.
  • In a normal distribution about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations; a z-score measures distance from the mean in standard deviations.
  • A statistic varies from sample to sample. The sample mean is unbiased, its standard error is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), and by the central limit theorem its distribution is approximately normal for large \(n\).
  • A 95% confidence interval, \(\bar{x} \pm t\,s/\sqrt{n}\), comes from a method that captures the parameter in 95% of samples. The bootstrap gives intervals for almost any statistic.
  • A hypothesis test computes a p-value: the probability, under \(H_0\), of a result at least as extreme as observed. Welch's t-test and the permutation test compare two means; the chi-square test compares categorical proportions.
  • Type I errors are false positives (rate \(\alpha\)); type II errors are missed effects. Power rises with sample size and effect size.
  • Report effect sizes with confidence intervals, not only p-values; beware multiple testing.

docs.title: 7.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Check your answer by simulation.

Answer

The pairs with a total of 10, 11 or 12 are (4,6), (5,5), (6,4), (5,6), (6,5), (6,6): 6 of the 36 equally likely pairs, so the probability is \(6/36 = 1/6 \approx 0.167\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
t = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(100_000, 2)).sum(axis=1)
print((t >= 10).mean())

0.16754

Exercise 2

A call centre receives on average 3 calls per minute, and calls arrive independently. Using a Poisson model, find the probability of (a) no calls in a minute and (b) more than 5 calls in a minute.

Answer 
calls = stats.poisson(3)
print(round(calls.pmf(0), 4), round(1 - calls.cdf(5), 4))

0.0498 0.0839

(a) \(e^{-3} \approx 0.0498\); (b) about 0.084.

Exercise 3

Exam marks are roughly normal with mean 60 and standard deviation 12. What fraction of students score above 84? What mark separates the top 10%?

Answer

84 is two standard deviations above the mean, so about 2.3% score above it. The top 10% starts at the 90th percentile:

marks = stats.norm(60, 12)
print(round(1 - marks.cdf(84), 4), round(marks.ppf(0.9), 1))

0.0228 75.4

Exercise 4

A sample of 25 values has mean 48 and standard deviation 10. Compute a 95% confidence interval for the population mean. How would the interval change with a sample of 100 values with the same mean and standard deviation?

Answer 
for n in [25, 100]:
    se = 10 / np.sqrt(n)
    t = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n - 1)
    print(n, round(t, 3), round(48 - t * se, 2), round(48 + t * se, 2))

25 2.064 43.87 52.13
100 1.984 46.02 49.98

With \(n = 25\) the interval is about (43.9, 52.1). With \(n = 100\) the standard error halves (from 2 to 1) and the t value shrinks slightly, so the interval is about (46.0, 50.0), a little less than half as wide.

Exercise 5

A study reports "no significant difference (p = 0.32)" between two teaching methods, based on 8 students per method. Does this show the methods are equally effective?

Answer

No. A large p-value means the data is consistent with no difference, not that there is none. With 8 students per group the power is low, so even a real, meaningful difference would usually go undetected. The confidence interval for the difference would be wide, including both zero and sizeable effects in either direction; that interval is the honest summary.

Exercise 6

A researcher tests 40 different foods for an association with headaches, using \(\alpha = 0.05\) each time, and reports the two foods with \(p < 0.05\). If no food truly has any effect, how many "significant" results would be expected? What should the researcher do?

Answer

About \(40 \times 0.05 = 2\) false positives are expected even if no food has any effect, so finding two is exactly what chance predicts. The researcher should report all 40 tests, adjust for multiple testing (for example, the Bonferroni correction tests each at \(\alpha/40\)), and treat the two findings as hypotheses to check in new data.

docs.title: 7.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 7

Exercise 1

Which distribution models the number of heads in 20 tosses of a coin?

  1. Poisson
  2. binomial
  3. uniform
  4. normal
Answer

binomial

Exercise 2

About what fraction of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean?

  1. 0.68
  2. 0.90
  3. 0.95
  4. 0.997
Answer

0.95

Exercise 3

If the sample size is multiplied by 4, the standard error of the mean is

  1. unchanged
  2. halved
  3. quartered
  4. doubled
Answer

halved

Exercise 4

The central limit theorem says that, for large samples, the sample mean is approximately

  1. equal to the population mean
  2. normally distributed
  3. uniformly distributed
  4. skewed like the population
Answer

normally distributed

Exercise 5

A p-value is the probability of

  1. the null hypothesis being true
  2. data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true
  3. the alternative being true
  4. making a type II error
Answer

data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true

Exercise 6

Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a

  1. type I error
  2. type II error
  3. correct decision
  4. power
Answer

type I error

Exercise 7

In a bootstrap, resamples are drawn from the sample with or without replacement?

Answer

with / with replacement

Exercise 8

What does the bootstrap make possible that the t formula does not?

  1. intervals for statistics such as the median
  2. exact p-values
  3. larger samples
  4. removing bias from the data
Answer

intervals for statistics such as the median

docs.title: Chapter 2: Python Essentials for Data Work
docs.text:
The parts of the language that data work uses every day

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • use Python's basic types (numbers, strings, booleans, None) and know where floating-point arithmetic surprises;
  • store data in lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets, and choose between them;
  • index and slice sequences, including negative indexes;
  • write loops, conditions and comprehensions that filter and transform records;
  • define functions with default arguments and use them as sort keys;
  • read a small CSV text into a list of records, converting types and handling bad values;
  • use a few modules of the standard library that data work relies on.

This chapter is a working tour of Python for readers who have programmed a little, in Python or in another language. It does not try to cover the whole language. It covers what you need to read and write the code in the rest of the book, with examples drawn from data work: counting, filtering, summarising, and turning raw text into records. If Python is entirely new to you, read the chapter at the keyboard and type every example.

docs.title: 2.1 Values, types and variables
docs.text:
Every value in Python has a type. The ones you will meet constantly are:

Type Example values Used for int 0, 42, -7 counts, indexes float 3.14, -0.5, 1e6 measurements, averages str "Delhi", 'cups' text, labels, category names bool True, False the result of a comparison, a flag NoneType None "no value": missing or not yet known

Table 2.1. Python's basic types.

A variable is a name attached to a value with =. The name has no type of its own; it simply refers to whatever value was last assigned to it.

cups = 112                 # an int
price = 12.5               # a float
city = "Pune"              # a str
is_weekend = False         # a bool
revenue = cups * price
print(type(cups), type(price), type(city), type(is_weekend))
print("revenue:", revenue)

<class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'str'> <class 'bool'>
revenue: 1400.0

Arithmetic uses +, -, * and /. Division with / always gives a float. Two more operators are handy for counting: // is floor division (the whole number of times one number goes into another) and % is the remainder. ** raises to a power.

minutes = 135
print(minutes / 60)            # true division
print(minutes // 60, "hours and", minutes % 60, "minutes")
print(2 ** 10)

2.25
2 hours and 15 minutes
1024

docs.title: Floating-point numbers are approximations
docs.text:
A float stores a number in binary with about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits. Most decimal fractions, such as 0.1, have no exact binary form, so tiny rounding errors appear:

print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

0.30000000000000004
False
True

Caution: never test floats for exact equality

Compare floats with a tolerance, using math.isclose (or numpy.isclose for arrays, Chapter 3). The errors are tiny and do not matter for data analysis, but an == test that should be True can come out False.

docs.title: Comparisons and logic
docs.text:
Comparisons (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) produce booleans, which combine with and, or and not. None is tested with is None, not == None.

temperature = 38.4
print(temperature > 37.5 and temperature < 40)
print(37.5 < temperature < 40)       # chained comparison, same meaning
reading = None
print(reading is None)

True
True
True

docs.title: 2.2 Strings
docs.text:
Text is everywhere in data: names, categories, codes, dates before they are parsed, whole documents. A string is a sequence of characters in single or double quotes. Strings have methods, called with a dot, that return new strings (a string itself never changes).

raw = "  New Delhi  "
print(repr(raw.strip()))          # remove spaces at both ends
print(raw.strip().lower())
print(raw.strip().upper())
print(raw.strip().replace(" ", "_"))
print("a,b,,d".split(","))        # split on commas
print("-".join(["2024", "03", "15"]))
print("Delhi" in "New Delhi")     # substring test

'New Delhi'
new delhi
NEW DELHI
New_Delhi
['a', 'b', '', 'd']
2024-03-15
True

Cleaning text columns is mostly a matter of these few methods: strip the spaces, fix the case, replace unwanted characters, split into parts. Chapter 5 applies them to whole columns at once with pandas.

docs.title: f-strings
docs.text:
An f-string (a string with f before the quote) puts the values of expressions into text. A format code after a colon controls how numbers appear: .2f gives two decimals, , adds thousands separators, .1% shows a fraction as a percentage, and a number before the dot sets a minimum width.

mean_cups = 110.857142
share = 0.4231
total = 1234567
print(f"Mean cups per weekday: {mean_cups:.1f}")
print(f"Share of sales on weekends: {share:.1%}")
print(f"Total: {total:,}")
print(f"|{'left':<8}|{'right':>8}|{3.14159:>8.2f}|")

Mean cups per weekday: 110.9
Share of sales on weekends: 42.3%
Total: 1,234,567
|left    |   right|    3.14|

docs.title: 2.3 Lists and tuples
docs.text:
A list holds values in order, in square brackets. Lists can grow and shrink, and their elements can be changed. They are Python's general-purpose container for a sequence of data.

Elements are numbered from 0. A negative index counts from the end, so -1 is the last element. A slice a[start:stop] takes the elements from start up to but not including stop; either end can be left out. Figure 2.1 shows both.

temps = [21.5, 23.0, 19.8, 25.1, 24.4, 22.7]
print(temps[0], temps[-1])       # first and last
print(temps[1:4])                # indexes 1, 2, 3
print(temps[:2], temps[-2:])     # first two, last two
print(temps[::2])                # every second element
print(len(temps), min(temps), max(temps), round(sum(temps) / len(temps), 2))

21.5 22.7
[23.0, 19.8, 25.1]
[21.5, 23.0] [24.4, 22.7]
[21.5, 19.8, 24.4]
6 19.8 25.1 22.75

The half-open rule (stop is excluded) has a convenient consequence: temps[:k] and temps[k:] split the list into two parts with no overlap and nothing missing, and temps[a:b] has exactly b - a elements.

Lists are changed in place by methods such as append, extend, insert and sort, and by assigning to an index.

temps.append(20.9)
temps[2] = 19.9            # correct a reading
print(temps)
print(sorted(temps))       # a new sorted list; temps is unchanged
temps.sort(reverse=True)   # sorts temps itself
print(temps)

[21.5, 23.0, 19.9, 25.1, 24.4, 22.7, 20.9]
[19.9, 20.9, 21.5, 22.7, 23.0, 24.4, 25.1]
[25.1, 24.4, 23.0, 22.7, 21.5, 20.9, 19.9]

Caution: two names, one list

Assignment does not copy a list. After b = a, both names refer to the same list, and b.append(1) changes a too. Use b = a.copy() (or list(a)) when you need an independent copy. The same is true of dictionaries, NumPy arrays and pandas tables, and it is a frequent source of puzzling bugs.

A tuple is like a list but cannot be changed after it is made. It is written with round brackets, and is the natural type for a fixed group of values that belong together, such as one record:

record = ("Mon", 112)
day, cups = record          # unpacking
print(day, cups)

Mon 112

docs.title: 2.4 Dictionaries and sets
docs.text:
A dictionary maps keys to values. It answers "what is the value for this key?" instantly, however large it is. Keys are usually strings or numbers; values can be anything.

stock = {"tea": 40, "coffee": 25, "milk": 12}
print(stock["tea"])
stock["sugar"] = 30                # add a key
stock["milk"] -= 2                 # change a value
print(stock)
print(stock.get("juice", 0))       # a default when the key is missing
print("coffee" in stock)           # tests the keys
for item, qty in stock.items():
    if qty < 20:
        print("reorder", item)

40
{'tea': 40, 'coffee': 25, 'milk': 10, 'sugar': 30}
0
True
reorder milk

Reading a missing key with square brackets raises a KeyError; get with a default avoids it. A dictionary is the natural way to count things: go through the data, and add one to the count for each value.

orders = ["tea", "coffee", "tea", "tea", "juice", "coffee", "tea"]
counts = {}
for item in orders:
    counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1
print(counts)

from collections import Counter
print(Counter(orders).most_common(2))

{'tea': 4, 'coffee': 2, 'juice': 1}
[('tea', 4), ('coffee', 2)]

collections.Counter does the same counting in one line and adds useful methods such as most_common. pandas has the same idea for columns, value_counts (Chapter 4).

A set is an unordered collection of distinct values. It removes duplicates and tests membership quickly, and it supports the operations of set theory.

cities_a = {"Pune", "Delhi", "Chennai", "Pune"}
cities_b = {"Delhi", "Kolkata"}
print(sorted(cities_a))            # the duplicate is gone
print(cities_a & cities_b)         # intersection
print(sorted(cities_a | cities_b)) # union
print(sorted(cities_a - cities_b)) # in a but not in b

['Chennai', 'Delhi', 'Pune']
{'Delhi'}
['Chennai', 'Delhi', 'Kolkata', 'Pune']
['Chennai', 'Pune']
Container Written Ordered Changeable Duplicates Typical use list [1, 2, 2] yes yes allowed a sequence of values or records tuple (1, 2, 2) yes no allowed one fixed record dict {"a": 1} yes (insertion order) yes keys unique lookup by key, counting set {1, 2} no yes no distinct values, membership

Table 2.2. Python's four built-in containers compared.

docs.title: 2.5 Control flow
docs.text:
if, elif and else choose between blocks of code. The blocks are marked by indentation (four spaces by convention), not by brackets.

def grade(mark):
    if mark >= 75:
        return "distinction"
    elif mark >= 40:
        return "pass"
    else:
        return "fail"

for m in [82, 40, 39.5]:
    print(m, grade(m))

82 distinction
40 pass
39.5 fail

A for loop runs its block once for each element of a sequence. Three helpers make loops over data cleaner: range(n) gives the numbers 0 to n − 1, enumerate gives each element with its position, and zip walks through two or more sequences side by side.

days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
cups = [112, 98, 105]
for i, day in enumerate(days, start=1):
    print(i, day)
for day, c in zip(days, cups):
    print(f"{day}: {c} cups")

1 Mon
2 Tue
3 Wed
Mon: 112 cups
Tue: 98 cups
Wed: 105 cups

A while loop repeats as long as a condition holds. It is less common in data work, but useful when the number of repetitions is not known in advance:

balance, years = 1000.0, 0
while balance < 2000:
    balance *= 1.07        # grow by 7% a year
    years += 1
print(years, "years to double, ending at", round(balance, 2))

11 years to double, ending at 2104.85

docs.title: 2.6 Comprehensions
docs.text:
A list comprehension builds a new list from an old one in a single expression: [expression for item in sequence if condition]. It reads almost like the sentence "the expression for each item in the sequence, if the condition holds". It is the idiomatic way to transform and filter.

temps_c = [21.5, 23.0, 19.9, 25.1, 24.4, 22.7]
temps_f = [round(t * 9 / 5 + 32, 1) for t in temps_c]
warm = [t for t in temps_c if t > 23]
print(temps_f)
print(warm)

[70.7, 73.4, 67.8, 77.2, 75.9, 72.9]
[25.1, 24.4]

The same pattern makes dictionaries and sets:

names = ["asha", "ravi", "meena"]
lengths = {n.title(): len(n) for n in names}
initials = {n[0] for n in names}
print(lengths, sorted(initials))

{'Asha': 4, 'Ravi': 4, 'Meena': 5} ['a', 'm', 'r']

Key idea

Most data processing is a pipeline of filter (keep the rows that satisfy a condition), transform (compute a new value from each row) and aggregate (combine many values into one, such as a sum or a count). A comprehension does the first two; sum, len, min, max and friends do the third. pandas does all three on whole columns, which is why Chapter 4 feels familiar after this one.

docs.title: 2.7 Functions
docs.text:
A function packages a computation under a name so that it can be reused and tested. It takes arguments, and return sends back a result. A string just after the def line, the docstring, says what the function does.

def summarise(values, ndigits=2):
    """Return the count, mean and range of a list of numbers."""
    n = len(values)
    mean = sum(values) / n
    return n, round(mean, ndigits), max(values) - min(values)

n, m, r = summarise([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42])
print(n, m, r)
print(summarise([1, 2, 2], ndigits=4))

6 18.0 38
(3, 1.6667, 1)

ndigits=2 is a default argument: it is used when the caller does not give one. Returning several values actually returns one tuple, which the caller can unpack.

Functions are values too, so they can be passed to other functions. The commonest case in data work is a key function for sorting: sorted calls it on every element and sorts by the results. A short function can be written inline as a lambda.

people = [("Asha", 31), ("Ravi", 25), ("Meena", 42)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))               # by age
print(max(people, key=lambda p: p[1])[0], "is oldest")

[('Ravi', 25), ('Asha', 31), ('Meena', 42)]
Meena is oldest

docs.title: 2.8 Reading records from text
docs.text:
Data most often arrives as CSV (comma-separated values): plain text with one record per line and fields separated by commas, usually with a header line naming the fields. pandas reads CSV in one line (Chapter 4), but seeing it done by hand shows what can go wrong.

This book makes its data in code, so that every example runs without any files. io.StringIO wraps a string so that it behaves like an open file, which lets us use exactly the code we would use on a real file.

import csv
import io

text = """date,item,qty,price
2024-03-01,tea,3,12.5
2024-03-01,coffee,1,20
2024-03-02,tea,two,12.5
2024-03-02,juice,2,
2024-03-03,tea,4,12.5
"""

rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)))
print(len(rows), "rows")
print(rows[0])

5 rows
{'date': '2024-03-01', 'item': 'tea', 'qty': '3', 'price': '12.5'}

Every field arrives as a string, even the numbers, and two rows have problems: a quantity written as a word, and a missing price. A loop with try and except converts what it can and sets the rest aside, instead of crashing on the first bad value.

records, rejected = [], []
for row in rows:
    try:
        records.append({
            "date": row["date"],
            "item": row["item"],
            "qty": int(row["qty"]),
            "price": float(row["price"]),
        })
    except ValueError as err:
        rejected.append((row, str(err)))

print(len(records), "good,", len(rejected), "rejected")
for row, why in rejected:
    print(row["date"], row["item"], "->", why)

revenue = sum(r["qty"] * r["price"] for r in records)
print(f"revenue from good rows: {revenue:.2f}")

3 good, 2 rejected
2024-03-02 tea -> invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'two'
2024-03-02 juice -> could not convert string to float: ''
revenue from good rows: 107.50

int("two") and float("") both raise a ValueError, which the except clause catches. Keeping the rejected rows, with the reason, is much better than silently dropping them: you can count them, report them, and perhaps fix them by hand (the "two" is obviously 2).

Note: exceptions

An exception is Python's way of signalling an error: ValueError for a bad value, KeyError for a missing dictionary key, IndexError for an index past the end of a list, ZeroDivisionError, FileNotFoundError and many more. try ... except SomeError runs the code and handles that error if it happens. Catch the specific error you expect; a bare except: also hides genuine bugs.

docs.title: 2.9 Modules and the standard library
docs.text:
A module is a file of Python code that you load with import. Python ships with a large standard library of modules. A few are used in data work all the time:

import math
import statistics
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

print(math.sqrt(2), math.log(100, 10), math.pi)

marks = [62, 75, 58, 91, 75, 68]
print(statistics.mean(marks), statistics.median(marks), statistics.mode(marks))
print(round(statistics.stdev(marks), 2))

rng = random.Random(42)            # a seeded generator: the same numbers every run
print([rng.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(5)])

d = date(2024, 3, 15)
print(d + timedelta(days=30), d.strftime("%A"))

1.4142135623730951 2.0 3.141592653589793
71.5 71.5 75
11.74
[6, 1, 1, 6, 3]
2024-04-14 Friday

Note the seed given to the random number generator. Random numbers in a program are pseudo-random: a fixed algorithm produces them from a starting value, the seed. Fixing the seed makes the "random" results the same every time the program runs, which is essential for checking and reproducing an analysis (Chapter 13). NumPy has its own, faster generator, introduced in Chapter 3, which the rest of the book uses.

Libraries that do not come with Python, such as NumPy and pandas, are installed with pip (Section 1.5) and then imported in exactly the same way.

docs.title: 2.10 A worked example: summarising a sales log
docs.text:
This example puts the chapter together. Given the cleaned records of Section 2.8, we want total quantity and revenue per item, sorted by revenue.

totals = {}
for r in records:
    t = totals.setdefault(r["item"], {"qty": 0, "revenue": 0.0})
    t["qty"] += r["qty"]
    t["revenue"] += r["qty"] * r["price"]

ranked = sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]["revenue"], reverse=True)
print(f"{'item':<8}{'qty':>5}{'revenue':>10}")
for item, t in ranked:
    print(f"{item:<8}{t['qty']:>5}{t['revenue']:>10.2f}")

item      qty   revenue
tea         7     87.50
coffee      1     20.00

setdefault returns the value for a key, first inserting the given default if the key is missing; it saves an if statement. The pattern here, group by a key, then accumulate, is exactly what pandas' groupby does (Chapter 5), in one line and much faster on large data.

docs.title: 2.11 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • The basic types are int, float, str, bool and None. Floats are approximate: compare them with a tolerance.
  • Strings have methods (strip, lower, split, replace, join); f-strings format numbers for display.
  • Lists are ordered and changeable; tuples are fixed records; dictionaries look up and count by key; sets hold distinct values.
  • Indexes start at 0; negative indexes count from the end; a slice a[i:j] stops before j.
  • Assignment never copies a container: use .copy() when you need an independent one.
  • Comprehensions filter and transform; sum, len, min and max aggregate.
  • Functions package computations; key functions control sorting.
  • Raw text arrives as strings: convert types explicitly, catch ValueError, and keep a record of rejected rows.
  • Seed random number generators so that results can be reproduced.

docs.title: 2.12 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Without running it, say what [10, 20, 30, 40, 50][1:-1] gives, and how many elements a[3:7] has when a has at least 7 elements.

Answer

[20, 30, 40]: from index 1 up to but not including the last element. a[3:7] has 7 - 3 = 4 elements.

Exercise 2

Write a comprehension that turns [" Pune", "delhi ", "CHENNAI"] into ["Pune", "Delhi", "Chennai"].

Answer 
print([c.strip().title() for c in ["  Pune", "delhi ", "CHENNAI"]])

['Pune', 'Delhi', 'Chennai']

Exercise 3

Count the words of the sentence "the cat sat on the mat the end" with a dictionary, and print the most common word and its count.

Answer 
words = "the cat sat on the mat the end".split()
counts = {}
for w in words:
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
best = max(counts, key=counts.get)
print(best, counts[best])

the 3

max(counts, key=counts.get) goes through the keys and picks the one whose value is largest.

Exercise 4

After a = [1, 2, 3], b = a, c = a.copy() and b.append(4), what are a, b and c?

Answer

a and b are both [1, 2, 3, 4], because they are the same list; c is still [1, 2, 3], because it is a separate copy made before the append.

Exercise 5

Write a function to_float(s) that returns float(s) for a valid number and None for anything else (including an empty string). Apply it to ["3.5", "", "abc", "-2"].

Answer 
def to_float(s):
    try:
        return float(s)
    except ValueError:
        return None

print([to_float(s) for s in ["3.5", "", "abc", "-2"]])

[3.5, None, None, -2.0]

Exercise 6

Using zip, compute the total cost of a basket from qty = [2, 1, 5] and price = [30.0, 45.5, 8.0].

Answer 
qty = [2, 1, 5]
price = [30.0, 45.5, 8.0]
print(sum(q * p for q, p in zip(qty, price)))

145.5

\(2 \times 30 + 1 \times 45.5 + 5 \times 8 = 145.5\).

Exercise 7

Why does the book seed every random number generator it uses?

Answer

So that the "random" numbers, and therefore every result that depends on them, are the same each time the code runs. This lets readers reproduce the outputs shown, and lets an analyst check that a change in the result comes from a change in the code or data, not from different random draws.

docs.title: 2.13 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 2

Exercise 1

What does 17 // 5 evaluate to?

Answer

3

Exercise 2

What does 17 % 5 evaluate to?

Answer

2

Exercise 3

Which container should you use to count how often each word appears?

  1. list
  2. tuple
  3. dictionary
  4. set
Answer

dictionary

Exercise 4

If temps has 6 elements, which index refers to the last one?

  1. 6
  2. -1
  3. 0
  4. 5 and -1 both
Answer

5 and -1 both

Exercise 5

What is the type of every field read by csv.DictReader?

  1. int
  2. float
  3. str
  4. it depends on the value
Answer

str

Exercise 6

Which is the right way to compare two floats a and b?

  1. a == b
  2. math.isclose(a, b)
  3. a is b
  4. int(a) == int(b)
Answer

math.isclose(a, b)

Exercise 7

Which error does int("two") raise?

  1. TypeError
  2. KeyError
  3. ValueError
  4. IndexError
Answer

ValueError

docs.title: Chapter 8: Regression
docs.text:
Predicting a number: straight lines, many features, curves and regularisation

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

  • state the regression problem in terms of features, a target and a loss;
  • fit a simple linear regression by least squares, by formula and with scikit-learn, and interpret its slope and intercept;
  • measure fit and prediction error with residuals, MAE, RMSE and \(R^2\);
  • use scikit-learn's fit/predict interface with a train/test split and a baseline;
  • fit a multiple regression, including categorical features through one-hot encoding;
  • model curved relationships with polynomial features, and recognise overfitting;
  • explain what ridge and lasso regularisation do and when to use them.

So far we have described and compared data. From this chapter on we also predict. In regression the thing to be predicted, the target, is a number: the price of a house, the demand for electricity tomorrow, the time a delivery will take. The information used to predict it, the features, can be numbers or categories. A regression model is a rule that turns features into a predicted target, learned from examples where both are known. This is supervised learning: the examples supervise the learning by supplying the right answers.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

docs.title: 8.1 The regression problem
docs.text:
We write the features of one example as \(x\) (a single number, or a vector of several), the true target as \(y\), and the model's prediction as \(\hat{y}\) ("y hat"). The difference \(y - \hat{y}\) is the residual, or error, for that example. A good model makes the residuals small on examples it has not seen.

"Small" needs a definition, called the loss. The most common choice in regression is the squared error \((y - \hat{y})^2\), averaged over the examples:

\[ \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 . \]

Squaring makes all errors positive and punishes large errors much more than small ones. Its square root, the root mean squared error (RMSE), is in the same units as the target. The mean absolute error (MAE), \(\frac{1}{n}\sum |y_i - \hat{y}_i|\), is easier to explain ("on average the prediction is off by 12 thousand") and less dominated by a few large errors.

docs.title: 8.2 Simple linear regression
docs.text:
With one feature, the simplest model is a straight line:

\[ \hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x , \]

where \(b_0\) is the intercept (the prediction when \(x = 0\)) and \(b_1\) the slope (the change in prediction for each one-unit increase in \(x\)). Least squares chooses the \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. Calculus gives the answer in closed form:

\[ b_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x}. \]

The slope is the covariance of \(x\) and \(y\) divided by the variance of \(x\); equivalently \(b_1 = r\,s_y/s_x\), where \(r\) is the correlation of Section 6.6. The line always passes through the point of means \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\).

Here is a small dataset: the floor area and price of twelve flats in one neighbourhood (price in thousands of a currency unit).

area = np.array([45, 52, 60, 64, 70, 75, 82, 88, 95, 104, 110, 125])        # square metres
price = np.array([3100, 3350, 3900, 3800, 4500, 4400, 5100, 5000, 5900, 6100, 6800, 7300])

xbar, ybar = area.mean(), price.mean()
b1 = np.sum((area - xbar) * (price - ybar)) / np.sum((area - xbar) ** 2)
b0 = ybar - b1 * xbar
print(f"slope b1 = {b1:.2f}, intercept b0 = {b0:.1f}")

pred = b0 + b1 * area
resid = price - pred
print("residuals:", resid.round(0))
print(f"sum of residuals = {resid.sum():.6f}")

slope b1 = 54.77, intercept b0 = 510.6
residuals: [ 125.   -8.  103. -216.  156. -218.   99. -330.  187. -106.  265.  -56.]
sum of residuals = 0.000000

The slope says that, among these flats, each extra square metre goes with about 54 thousand more in price. The intercept is the line's value at zero area; it is needed to place the line but has no sensible meaning by itself, because no flat has zero area. Least-squares residuals always add up to zero (up to rounding): the line is balanced among the points.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
ax.scatter(area, price, zorder=3, label="flats")
xs = np.array([40, 130])
ax.plot(xs, b0 + b1 * xs, color="tab:orange", label=f"price = {b0:.0f} + {b1:.1f} x area")
for x, y, p in zip(area, price, pred):
    ax.plot([x, x], [y, p], color="gray", linewidth=1, linestyle=":")
ax.set_xlabel("Floor area (square metres)")
ax.set_ylabel("Price (thousands)")
ax.set_title("Least-squares line; dotted lines are residuals")
ax.legend()
fig.savefig("regression-line.svg")
Figure 8.1 A least-squares line and its residuals. A scatter plot of price against floor area for twelve flats, rising steadily from about 3,100 at 45 square metres to 7,300 at 125. The fitted least-squares line passes through the middle of the points, and a short dotted vertical line joins each point to the line, showing its residual.

docs.title: How good is the fit? R²
docs.text:
The coefficient of determination, \(R^2\), compares the model's squared error with that of the simplest possible prediction, the mean \(\bar{y}\) for everyone:

\[ R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}. \]

\(R^2 = 1\) means perfect predictions; \(R^2 = 0\) means no better than predicting the mean; on new data it can even be negative, meaning worse than the mean. For a simple linear regression on the data it was fitted to, \(R^2\) equals \(r^2\), the squared correlation.

ss_res = np.sum(resid ** 2)
ss_tot = np.sum((price - ybar) ** 2)
print(f"R^2 = {1 - ss_res / ss_tot:.4f}, r^2 = {np.corrcoef(area, price)[0, 1] ** 2:.4f}")
print(f"RMSE = {np.sqrt(np.mean(resid ** 2)):.1f}, MAE = {np.mean(np.abs(resid)):.1f}")

R^2 = 0.9810, r^2 = 0.9810
RMSE = 178.6, MAE = 155.8

Floor area explains about 98% of the variation in these prices, and a typical prediction is off by about 150 thousand. These are measures of fit on the same data the line was fitted to; Section 8.3 measures error on new data, which is what matters for prediction.

Caution: extrapolation

A fitted line describes the data in the range it came from. Predicting a 300-square-metre flat from data that stops at 125 assumes the straight line continues far beyond the evidence. Large flats may be priced quite differently. Be wary of any prediction outside the range of the training data.

docs.title: 8.3 Regression with scikit-learn
docs.text:
scikit-learn provides hundreds of models with one consistent interface. Every model is an object (an estimator) that is created with its settings, trained with fit(X, y), and used with predict(X). X is a two-dimensional table of features (one row per example, one column per feature) and y a one-dimensional array of targets.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X = area.reshape(-1, 1)          # 12 rows, 1 feature column
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, price)
print(model.intercept_.round(1), model.coef_.round(2))
print(model.predict(np.array([[50], [100]])).round(0))
print(round(model.score(X, price), 4))       # R^2

510.6 [54.77]
[3249. 5987.]
0.981

The results match the formulas. Fitted values are stored in attributes ending in an underscore (coef_, intercept_). score returns \(R^2\) for regressors.

docs.title: Training data and test data
docs.text:
A model's error on the data it was trained on is optimistic: the model has adapted to those very examples, including their noise. To estimate how it will do on new cases, hold some data back. Split the data at random into a training set, used to fit the model, and a test set, used only to evaluate it. Chapter 10 develops this into cross-validation; for now a single split is enough.

To have enough data for a fair split we generate a larger, more realistic dataset of 400 houses with several features. As always, the generating rules are known to us but would not be in real life.

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
n = 400
houses = pd.DataFrame({
    "area": rng.uniform(40, 200, n).round(0),
    "bedrooms": rng.integers(1, 6, n),
    "age": rng.uniform(0, 50, n).round(0),
    "location": rng.choice(["centre", "suburb", "outskirts"], n, p=[0.3, 0.45, 0.25]),
})
loc_effect = houses["location"].map({"centre": 1500, "suburb": 500, "outskirts": 0})
houses["price"] = (800 + 45 * houses["area"] + 150 * houses["bedrooms"] - 20 * houses["age"]
                   + loc_effect + rng.normal(0, 400, n)).round(0)
print(houses.head())
print(houses.describe().round(1).loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]])

    area  bedrooms   age   location   price
0   92.0         2  50.0     suburb  4295.0
1  198.0         1  42.0     suburb  9520.0
2   91.0         5  27.0     centre  5734.0
3  166.0         1  34.0     suburb  8077.0
4  179.0         5  30.0  outskirts  9348.0
       area  bedrooms   age    price
mean  119.4       2.9  24.4   6790.3
std    44.0       1.4  14.1   2122.7
min    41.0       1.0   0.0   2057.0
max   200.0       5.0  50.0  11272.0

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, root_mean_squared_error, r2_score

X = houses[["area"]]
y = houses["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
print(len(X_train), "training rows,", len(X_test), "test rows")

simple = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = simple.predict(X_test)
print(f"test MAE  = {mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred):.1f}")
print(f"test RMSE = {root_mean_squared_error(y_test, pred):.1f}")
print(f"test R^2  = {r2_score(y_test, pred):.3f}")

300 training rows, 100 test rows
test MAE  = 643.7
test RMSE = 798.6
test R^2  = 0.866

random_state seeds the random split so that it is the same every time. The metrics come from sklearn.metrics, which always takes the true values first and the predictions second.

docs.title: Always compare with a baseline
docs.text:
Is an MAE of several hundred good? It depends on how hard the problem is. A baseline answers that: the error of a trivial model that ignores the features, such as predicting the training mean for every house. scikit-learn's DummyRegressor does exactly this.

from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor

baseline = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"baseline test MAE = {mean_absolute_error(y_test, baseline.predict(X_test)):.1f}")
print(f"baseline test R^2 = {r2_score(y_test, baseline.predict(X_test)):.3f}")

baseline test MAE = 1874.3
baseline test R^2 = -0.000

Floor area alone cuts the baseline error by a large factor. A model that cannot beat the baseline has learned nothing useful, however sophisticated it is.

docs.title: 8.4 Multiple regression
docs.text:
With several features \(x_1, \dots, x_p\) the linear model becomes

\[ \hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_p x_p , \]

still fitted by least squares. Each coefficient \(b_j\) is now the change in prediction for a one-unit increase in \(x_j\) with the other features held fixed. That qualification matters: in the simple regression, the area coefficient also absorbed the effect of anything that goes with area, such as the number of bedrooms.

docs.title: Categorical features: one-hot encoding
docs.text:
A model needs numbers, but location is text. One-hot encoding replaces a categorical column with one 0/1 column per category. To avoid redundancy (the columns would always add up to 1), one category is usually dropped and becomes the reference; each remaining coefficient is then the difference from the reference category.

encoded = pd.get_dummies(houses[["area", "bedrooms", "age", "location"]], columns=["location"],
                         drop_first=True, dtype=int)
print(encoded.head(3))

    area  bedrooms   age  location_outskirts  location_suburb
0   92.0         2  50.0                   0                1
1  198.0         1  42.0                   0                1
2   91.0         5  27.0                   0                0

With drop_first=True pandas drops the first category in alphabetical order, here centre, which becomes the reference. location_outskirts is 1 for houses on the outskirts and location_suburb is 1 for houses in the suburbs; a house in the centre has 0 in both. Checking the column names confirms it:

print(encoded.columns.tolist())

['area', 'bedrooms', 'age', 'location_outskirts', 'location_suburb']

Now fit the multiple regression on the same split:

X_all = encoded
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_all, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
multi = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print(pd.Series(multi.coef_, index=X_all.columns).round(1))
print("intercept", round(multi.intercept_, 1))
pred = multi.predict(X_test)
print(f"test MAE = {mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred):.1f}, test R^2 = {r2_score(y_test, pred):.3f}")

area                    44.7
bedrooms               159.2
age                    -20.9
location_outskirts   -1450.3
location_suburb       -924.9
dtype: float64
intercept 2286.3
test MAE = 344.4, test R^2 = 0.962

The coefficients recover the rules used to generate the data, within the noise: about 45 per square metre, 150 per bedroom, \(-20\) per year of age; houses on the outskirts about 1,500 cheaper and in the suburbs about 1,000 cheaper than comparable houses in the centre (the reference). The test error falls well below that of area alone.

Key idea

A coefficient in a multiple regression is a conditional effect: the difference in prediction for one unit of that feature among examples that are alike in all the other features in the model. Add or remove a feature and the other coefficients can change. And a coefficient describes the data, not necessarily a cause: in observational data, a feature may stand in for something unmeasured.

docs.title: Residual plots
docs.text:
A plot of residuals against predicted values checks whether a straight-line model is adequate. If it is, the residuals form a shapeless band around zero. A curve suggests a missing non-linear term; a funnel shape suggests that the errors grow with the size of the prediction.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.scatter(pred, y_test - pred, s=12, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(0, color="gray")
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted price")
ax.set_ylabel("Residual (actual - predicted)")
ax.set_title("Residuals of the multiple regression (test set)")
fig.savefig("residuals.svg")
Figure 8.2 A healthy residual plot. A scatter plot of residuals against predicted prices for the test houses. The points form an even horizontal band around the zero line, from about -1,000 to +1,000, with no curve or funnel.

Here the residuals show no pattern, as expected, since the data was generated by a linear rule plus noise.

docs.title: 8.5 Curves: polynomial regression and overfitting
docs.text:
A straight line cannot follow a curved relationship. One way to fit curves while keeping the machinery of linear regression is to add powers of a feature as new features: \(x^2\), \(x^3\), and so on. The model \(\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2\) is still linear in the coefficients, so least squares fits it in exactly the same way.

scikit-learn's PolynomialFeatures creates the powers, and a pipeline chains it with the regression so that the steps behave as one model. A StandardScaler in between rescales the powers (Section 8.6 explains it); without it, numbers like \(10^{15}\) next to numbers like 1 make the computation numerically unreliable at high degrees.

from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
x = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 10, 20))
y_curve = 2 + 1.5 * x - 0.12 * x ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 20)     # a gentle curve plus noise
x_new = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 10, 200))                            # fresh data from the same source
y_new = 2 + 1.5 * x_new - 0.12 * x_new ** 2 + rng.normal(0, 0.8, 200)

for degree in [1, 2, 15]:
    poly = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())
    poly.fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y_curve)
    train_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(y_curve, poly.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1)))
    new_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(y_new, poly.predict(x_new.reshape(-1, 1)))
    print(f"degree {degree:>2}: training RMSE {train_rmse:.3f}, new-data RMSE {new_rmse:.3f}")

degree  1: training RMSE 1.095, new-data RMSE 1.170
degree  2: training RMSE 0.763, new-data RMSE 0.851
degree 15: training RMSE 0.618, new-data RMSE 3.432

grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 400).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2), sharey=True)
for ax, degree, title in zip(axes, [1, 2, 15], ["underfit", "about right", "overfit"]):
    poly = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y_curve)
    ax.scatter(x, y_curve, s=15)
    ax.plot(grid, poly.predict(grid), color="tab:orange")
    ax.set_ylim(-1, 9)
    ax.set_title(f"degree {degree}: {title}")
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
axes[0].set_ylabel("y")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("polynomial-fits.svg")
Figure 8.3 Underfitting, a good fit and overfitting. Three panels showing the same 20 points, which follow a gentle hump. A straight line (degree 1) misses the curvature. A degree-2 curve follows the hump smoothly. A degree-15 polynomial wiggles through many individual points and swings wildly near the ends.

The numbers and the picture tell the central story of all machine learning:

  • The straight line underfits: it is too simple to capture the curve, so its error is high on both training and new data. This is bias.
  • Degree 2 matches the true shape and has the lowest error on new data.
  • Degree 15 overfits: it bends to follow the noise in the 20 training points, so its training error is the lowest of all, but on new data it does worse than degree 2, with wild swings near the edges. This is variance: the fit would change a lot with a different sample.

Caution: training error always falls as complexity rises

Adding features or flexibility can only lower the error on the training data, so training error cannot be used to choose a model's complexity. Use held-out data: a test set, or the cross-validation of Chapter 10.

docs.title: 8.6 Regularisation: ridge and lasso
docs.text:
Overfitting shows up as coefficients that are very large, balancing each other to chase the noise. Regularisation discourages this by adding a penalty on the size of the coefficients to the loss. Ridge regression minimises

\[ \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \alpha \sum_j b_j^2 , \]

and lasso regression uses \(\alpha \sum_j |b_j|\) instead. The hyperparameter \(\alpha \ge 0\) sets the strength of the penalty: \(\alpha = 0\) gives ordinary least squares, and a large \(\alpha\) shrinks the coefficients towards zero. The lasso can shrink some coefficients exactly to zero, effectively selecting features. (The intercept is not penalised.)

Because the penalty adds up the coefficients of different features, the features should be on comparable scales, so regularised models are almost always preceded by standardisation (Section 3.7), done by StandardScaler.

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso

for name, reg in [("plain", LinearRegression()), ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1.0)), ("lasso", Lasso(alpha=0.01, max_iter=50_000))]:
    pipe = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(15), StandardScaler(), reg)
    pipe.fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y_curve)
    coefs = pipe[-1].coef_
    new_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(y_new, pipe.predict(x_new.reshape(-1, 1)))
    print(f"{name:>5}: new-data RMSE {new_rmse:.3f}, largest |coef| {np.abs(coefs).max():10.1f}, "
          f"zero coefs {np.sum(np.abs(coefs) < 1e-8)}")

plain: new-data RMSE 3.432, largest |coef|    14745.0, zero coefs 1
ridge: new-data RMSE 0.965, largest |coef|        1.2, zero coefs 1
lasso: new-data RMSE 0.902, largest |coef|        2.1, zero coefs 13

With the same degree-15 features, ridge and lasso keep the coefficients small and the error on new data comes back close to that of the well-chosen degree-2 model. The lasso has set most of the 16 coefficients to exactly zero, keeping only a few powers. (One coefficient is zero in every row: PolynomialFeatures adds a constant column of ones, which becomes a column of zeros after scaling and so gets no weight; the intercept does its job.) The right \(\alpha\) is found by trying several values on held-out data, which is the subject of Chapter 10.

docs.title: 8.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Regression predicts a numerical target from features, learned from examples (supervised learning). Residuals are actual minus predicted.
  • Least squares minimises the sum of squared residuals. For one feature, \(b_1 = \sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) / \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\) and \(b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x}\).
  • MAE and RMSE measure error in the target's units; \(R^2\) compares the model with predicting the mean.
  • scikit-learn estimators share fit(X, y), predict(X) and score; evaluate on a held-out test set and against a DummyRegressor baseline.
  • In multiple regression each coefficient is an effect with the other features held fixed. Encode categories one-hot, dropping a reference category.
  • Residual plots reveal curvature and changing spread.
  • Polynomial features fit curves; too little flexibility underfits (bias), too much overfits (variance). Training error cannot choose the complexity.
  • Ridge and lasso penalise large coefficients; standardise features first; lasso can zero out coefficients. Choose \(\alpha\) on held-out data.

docs.title: 8.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

For the points \((1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6)\), compute the least-squares slope and intercept by hand, and check with NumPy.

Answer

\(\bar{x} = 2.5\), \(\bar{y} = 4\). The deviations of \(x\) are \(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5\) and of \(y\) are \(-2, -1, 1, 2\). \(\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y}) = 3 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 3 = 7\) and \(\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5\). So \(b_1 = 7/5 = 1.4\) and \(b_0 = 4 - 1.4 \times 2.5 = 0.5\).

print(np.polyfit([1, 2, 3, 4], [2, 3, 5, 6], deg=1))

[1.4 0.5]

np.polyfit returns the coefficients from the highest power down: slope 1.4, intercept 0.5.

Exercise 2

A model has test \(R^2 = -0.15\). What does that mean?

Answer

On the test data the model's squared error is 15% larger than that of simply predicting the mean target for every example. It is worse than the trivial baseline, usually because it overfits the training data or because the test data differs from the training data.

Exercise 3

In the multiple regression on houses, the coefficient of bedrooms is about 150. A friend concludes, "adding a bedroom to a house raises its value by 150 thousand." What is right and what is wrong with that?

Answer

Right: among houses with the same area, age and location in this data, each extra bedroom goes with about 150 thousand more in predicted price. Wrong, or at least unsupported: this is an association in data, not the result of adding bedrooms to houses. Adding a bedroom without changing the area means making the other rooms smaller, which is not what the data compares. In this simulated data we built the effect in, but with real data a causal claim would need more than a regression coefficient.

Exercise 4

Fit a simple regression of price on age alone for the houses data, using the same split as Section 8.3 (test_size=0.25, random_state=0), and compare its test MAE with the baseline's.

Answer 
Xa = houses[["age"]]
Xa_tr, Xa_te, ya_tr, ya_te = train_test_split(Xa, houses["price"], test_size=0.25, random_state=0)
age_model = LinearRegression().fit(Xa_tr, ya_tr)
print(round(age_model.coef_[0], 1))
print(round(mean_absolute_error(ya_te, age_model.predict(Xa_te)), 1))
print(round(mean_absolute_error(ya_te, DummyRegressor().fit(Xa_tr, ya_tr).predict(Xa_te)), 1))

-2.3
1868.0
1874.3

Age alone barely improves on the baseline. Its fitted slope, about \(-2\) per year, is also far from the \(-20\) per year that generated the data. Age's true effect (at most about 1,000 across the whole age range) is small compared with the variation in price driven by area, and when area is left out, that variation stays in the residuals and makes the age slope very imprecise. A feature can matter in a multiple regression and still be poorly estimated, and predict poorly, on its own.

Exercise 5

Why must features be standardised before ridge or lasso regression, but not before ordinary least squares?

Answer

Ordinary least squares gives the same predictions whatever the units of the features: rescaling a feature just rescales its coefficient. The ridge and lasso penalties add up the sizes of the coefficients, so a feature measured in small units (needing a large coefficient) would be penalised more than the same feature in large units. Standardising puts all features on the same scale so that the penalty treats them equally.

Exercise 6

Explain in your own words why the degree-15 polynomial has the lowest training error but not the lowest error on new data.

Answer

With 16 coefficients and only 20 points, the polynomial is flexible enough to bend towards each training point, fitting the random noise as well as the underlying curve. That lowers the training error, but the noise in new data is different, so the bends that fitted the old noise are wrong for the new points, especially near the ends of the range where the polynomial swings. The degree-2 model cannot follow the noise, so what it learns is closer to the true shape that the new data shares.

docs.title: 8.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 8

  1. the origin
  2. the point of means
  3. the first data point
  4. the largest residual

Exercise 2

  2. MAE
  3. R squared

Exercise 3

  1. perfect
  2. as good as predicting the mean
  3. useless and harmful
  4. overfitting
Answer

Exercise 4

  1. predict
  2. fit
  3. score
  4. transform
Answer

Exercise 5

A model with very low training error and high test error is

  1. underfitting
  2. overfitting
  3. a baseline
  4. regularised
Answer

  1. ridge
  2. lasso
  3. least squares
  4. polynomial features
